markerNotes: Spatial distribution is about where the hazard is, and nature is about how it behaves. Describe both, and anchor each with a feature from the hazard map or records.
Speed of onset matters for a flash flood: the time between the rain and the rise is what makes the hazard hard to manage.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the flood in general terms without referring to the hazard map or the rainfall records supplied.
Confusing the spatial distribution with the cause of the flood.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes where the hazard occurs (its spatial distribution across the upper and lower catchment, linked to the hazard map) and its nature (intensity, duration and speed of onset, linked to the rainfall records), with at least one specific feature from the scenario
3 marks: Describes either the spatial distribution or the nature of the hazard with some supporting detail
2 marks: Names the hazard and one feature of its location or behaviour without description
1 mark: Makes a general statement that floods are dangerous

sampleAnswers.answer: The contemporary hazard in Pellow Creek is spread across the catchment in two linked parts. The hazard map shows that flood extent covers the lower catchment, while the rainfall records show intense, short bursts of rain falling on the steep upper slopes. The nature of the flash flood hazard is defined by its speed: heavy bursts of rain produce a rapid rise in flow, so the time between rainfall and flooding is brief. The spatial distribution and nature together explain why flooding occurs in the lower catchment after rain that falls higher up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the spatial distribution from the hazard map (lower catchment) and the nature from the rainfall records (intense, short bursts on steep upper slopes), with the speed of onset as a specific feature. The closing link between distribution and nature is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flash flood hazard in Pellow Creek affects the township in the lower catchment.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the hazard and one feature of its location without describing either part in detail, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Floods are dangerous to people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no reference to the catchment or the data, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The hypothetical Pellow Creek catchment has experienced repeated flash floods in recent years. A hazard map shows flood extent across the lower catchment, and rainfall records show intense short bursts of rain falling on steep upper slopes. The catchment, map and records are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Classify the Pellow Creek flash flood by its type (natural or ecological) and by its spatial extent (local or regional scale), giving a reason for each classification.
markerNotes: A classification needs a basis. Name the criterion (origin of the hazard, or the area it affects) before giving the class.
A scale claim must be tested against the scenario: the flood is local because it is confined to one valley, not because it is small.
commonStudentErrors: Calling a flash flood ecological because it changes the environment, when its origin is physical.
Classifying the spatial extent as regional without checking whether other sub-catchments flood at the same time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies the flash flood as a natural hazard, classifies its spatial extent at the local scale, and gives a reason for each classification tied to the scenario
2 marks: Classifies the hazard by type or by scale, with one supporting reason
1 mark: Makes a classification with no reason, or a classification that is incorrect

sampleAnswers.answer: The Pellow Creek flash flood is a natural hazard, because it originates in intense rainfall on the steep upper slopes rather than in the disturbance of living systems. Its spatial extent is at the local scale, because the flooding is confined to the lower valley and the township beside the creek, and no other sub-catchment floods at the same time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies the flash flood by origin (natural) and by extent (local), with a reason for each tied to the scenario: the flooding is confined to the lower valley and township, and no other sub-catchment floods at the same time.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flash flood is a natural hazard because it is caused by heavy rain. It is at a local scale in Pellow Creek.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies both the type and the scale, but gives a reason only for the type. The scale is stated without a reason, so it sits at 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flash flood is an ecological hazard.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The classification is incorrect and has no reason, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical hazard briefing for Pellow Creek describes flooding that is confined to the lower valley and the township beside the creek. The rain that causes it falls on the steep upper slopes of the same catchment, and no other sub-catchment floods at the same time. The briefing is hypothetical.

dotPoints.description: Characteristics of the natural environment, including the physical processes and cycles influencing the nature and occurrence of the hazard

prompts.question: Define a flash flood, and name one physical process that influences the occurrence of flash flooding in the hypothetical Pellow Creek catchment.
markerNotes: A definition of a flash flood needs three features: rapid rise, short time frame and intense rain. Two of the three is not enough for full marks.
The physical process should be specific to the catchment, such as saturated soil on thin slopes, rather than a general statement about rain.
commonStudentErrors: Defining a flash flood as any flood, with no reference to speed or time.
Naming a human process such as land clearing in a question that asks for a physical process.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Defines a flash flood as a rapid rise in water level in a stream after intense rainfall over a short period, and names one physical process (such as saturated soil or intense rainfall) that influences its occurrence in the catchment
1 mark: Defines the flash flood correctly or names one physical process, but not both

sampleAnswers.answer: A flash flood is a rapid rise in water level within hours of intense rainfall. In Pellow Creek, saturated soil on steep slopes is a physical process of the natural environment that influences the occurrence of the hazard.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines the flash flood with a rapid rise in water level, a short time frame and intense rainfall, and names a specific physical process (saturated soil on steep slopes) for Pellow Creek. Both parts earn full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A flash flood is when a river rises fast after heavy rain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The definition is largely correct, but no physical process is named, so it earns the 1-mark level.

prompts.question: Explain how the physical processes and cycles of the Pellow Creek catchment, including its rainfall and soil conditions, influence the nature and occurrence of the flash flood hazard.
markerNotes: The top band chains the processes: rain intensity meets soil capacity on steep slopes, which sets the speed of the rise, and antecedent wetness sets when floods occur.
Naming the processes is not enough. Each one needs a stated effect on either the nature or the occurrence of the hazard.
commonStudentErrors: Listing rainfall, soils and slopes without saying how each one changes the hazard.
Describing the hazard's impacts on people rather than the physical processes that cause it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how specific physical processes (rainfall intensity, soil saturation, slope and the water cycle) interact to determine the nature (rate of rise, speed of onset) and occurrence (frequency and timing) of the flash flood, with a clear causal chain and a reference to the catchment
4 marks: Explains how two physical processes influence the nature or occurrence of the hazard, with a causal link
3 marks: Identifies physical processes and cycles in the catchment with limited explanation of their effect on the hazard
2 marks: Names one physical process without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about weather

sampleAnswers.answer: Physical processes and cycles in the Pellow Creek catchment combine to shape the flash flood hazard. Rainfall intensity is the trigger: the water cycle delivers intense summer storms that drop large volumes of rain in a short period. On the steep upper slopes, thin soils cannot absorb this rain quickly, so runoff flows straight into the channel. This determines the nature of the hazard, giving a rapid rate of rise and short warning time. Soils already saturated from earlier storms have less capacity to absorb new rain, so the occurrence of flooding depends on how often summer storms arrive in quick succession. Together these processes explain both how quickly the creek rises and when flooding is most likely, and the hazard map shows where this runoff concentrates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Chains rainfall intensity, steep slopes and thin soils into the nature of the hazard (rate of rise), then shows how soil saturation from earlier storms governs its occurrence. Each process has a stated effect, which is the top-band requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The creek rises quickly because the upper slopes are steep and the soils are thin, so rain runs off. Intense rain is the main trigger for the flood.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies slope, soil and rainfall as physical processes with some effect on the hazard, but the explanation is limited and the cycles are not discussed, so it sits at 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rain causes the creek to flood.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about weather with no physical process explained, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: Pellow Creek's catchment has steep upper slopes with thin soils. The water cycle delivers intense summer storms that can drop large volumes of rain in a short period, and the hazard map shows where runoff concentrates. The Pellow Creek catchment is hypothetical.

dotPoints.description: Human–environment interactions and evidence of change

prompts.question: Analyse the contribution of human activities to hazard events in Pellow Creek, and how the evidence of change in the flood record relates to climate.
markerNotes: Analyse means showing how the human and climate influences combine. Two separate causes listed side by side are a description, not an analysis.
A strong answer names the limit of the evidence, such as needing a longer rainfall record, before drawing a firm conclusion about cause.
commonStudentErrors: Blaming people for all floods without acknowledging the natural rainfall trigger.
Treating climate and human land use as separate causes, with no interaction between them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Analyses how human activities (clearing, paving and drainage changes) increase runoff and so contribute to hazard events, relates the evidence of change in the flood record to climate, and explains how the two influences interact, with reference to the scenario
4 marks: Explains one human contribution to flood events and relates the evidence of change to climate, without showing how the two interact
3 marks: Describes evidence of change in the flood record with one human activity identified, and limited explanation
2 marks: Names one human activity or one piece of evidence without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that people cause floods

sampleAnswers.answer: Human activities contribute to flash flood hazard events in Pellow Creek mainly by changing how water moves across the catchment. Clearing of the upper slopes and the expansion of paved surfaces reduce infiltration, and any drainage changes would concentrate runoff further, so more rain runs off directly into the channel. The evidence of change in the flood record, with flash floods becoming more frequent over the last two decades, coincides with this development. The rainfall records also show more heavy bursts in recent years, and a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, so climate may be intensifying those bursts. These human–environment interactions are therefore amplified: development makes each burst more damaging, while climate may make the bursts more frequent. Separating the two causes requires a longer rainfall record.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how clearing and paving reduce infiltration and so increase runoff, relates the flood record to climate, and shows the two influences interact so that each burst is more damaging. The limitation about separating the causes shows the analysis is tested against the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: Flash floods have become more frequent in Pellow Creek, and paved surfaces and cleared slopes are one human activity that has expanded. Rainfall records also show more heavy bursts. The flood record therefore shows change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the evidence of change and identifies one human activity, but the explanation of how the activity affects runoff is limited and climate is not related, so it sits at 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: People cause floods by building things.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no evidence and no specific activity named, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: Flood records for Pellow Creek show flash floods becoming more frequent over the last two decades, the same period in which paved surfaces and cleared slopes have expanded across the catchment. Rainfall records show more heavy bursts in recent years. The Pellow Creek records are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Deduce from the Pellow Creek flood records whether the frequency of flash floods is likely to increase, using the trend in heavy rainfall bursts as evidence.
markerNotes: Deduce means reasoning from the data to a conclusion the data supports. The conclusion should follow from a named trend, not from general knowledge.
A limitation of the inference, such as four decades from one station, is what separates a 3 from a 2.
commonStudentErrors: Stating a prediction with no link to the data in the table.
Treating two rising trends as proof that one causes the other, with no caveat.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Deduces a likely increase in flash flood frequency from the trend in heavy rainfall bursts, sets out the reasoning step by step from the data, and notes one limitation of the inference
2 marks: Deduces a direction of change from the data with a brief reason
1 mark: States a conclusion with no reasoning from the data

sampleAnswers.answer: In Pellow Creek, the flood records show flash floods rising over four decades, and the heavy rainfall bursts rise over the same period. Because both series move together, the trend in heavy rainfall bursts is the most likely driver of the rising frequency, so the evidence supports deducing that flash floods will become more frequent. However, four decades is a short record, so a run of wet years could exaggerate the trend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Works from the two rising trends to a deduction about frequency, states why the rainfall trend is the more likely driver, and notes a clear limitation (a short four-decade record). The reasoning is traceable to the table.

sampleAnswers.answer: Flash floods are rising, and heavy rainfall is rising too, so floods will probably become more frequent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Deduces a direction of change from the data with a brief reason, but there is no step-by-step reasoning or limitation, so it sits at 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Floods are becoming more common in Pellow Creek.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States a conclusion without reasoning from the table, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical table lists flash flood warnings and heavy rainfall bursts in Pellow Creek for four decades. Both columns rise across the period. The table is hypothetical.

dotPoints.description: Challenges, opportunities and responses

prompts.question: Discuss the challenges and opportunities that the Pellow Creek flash flood presents for the township, including the varying perspectives of residents, the council and insurers, and the responses at more than one scale.
markerNotes: Discuss means arguing both sides of each option. Show that the residents, council and insurers each have a reasonable view, then judge the trade-offs.
Top answers match each response to a scale: a levee acts locally, a warning system across the township, and a buy-back on the catchment floodplain.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the three options with no discussion of their trade-offs.
Treating insurers' or the council's view as the only valid perspective.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses challenges and opportunities for the township with specific evidence, weighs the varying perspectives of residents, the council and insurers, and explains responses at more than one scale, reaching a reasoned conclusion on the trade-offs
5 marks: Discusses challenges and opportunities with some evidence, outlines the perspectives of at least two groups, and explains one response at one scale
4 marks: Discusses one challenge and one opportunity with limited evidence, and identifies one response
3 marks: Describes challenges or opportunities with little discussion of responses or perspectives
2 marks: Names one challenge or one response without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about flood impacts

sampleAnswers.answer: The Pellow Creek flash flood presents challenges for the township that are both physical and social. Repeated floods damage homes, and the rapid rise leaves residents little time to respond, so warning and preparation matter as much as the flood itself. The opportunities lie in the responses on offer: a warning system can reduce risk across the township, a buy-back can remove the most flood-prone homes from the hazard, and a levee can protect the homes behind it. The varying perspectives of residents, the council and insurers may shape which option is chosen. Residents may favour a levee, the council may favour a township-wide warning system, and insurers may favour buy-backs. Each view is reasonable, but it reflects a different scale of response: a levee works on the creek reach, a warning system across the township, and a buy-back on individual homes. The judgement turns on these trade-offs, and a combination is often most defensible, since warnings give immediate protection while catchment management of runoff from the upper slopes addresses the longer-term cause.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses both the physical and social challenges and the opportunities, weighs each group's reasonable perspective, and matches each response to a scale. The conclusion on trade-offs and the link to catchment management earn the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flood is a challenge because it damages homes and gives residents little time to respond. An opportunity is a warning system that is cheap. Residents, the council and insurers may disagree about the best response, and a buy-back is one response that works at catchment scale.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses one challenge and one opportunity with limited evidence, and identifies responses and perspectives without weighing them. This matches the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flood damages homes and roads.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about impacts with no discussion of opportunities, perspectives or responses, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: After repeated flash floods, the Pellow Creek township is considering three options: a local levee, a township-wide warning system and a voluntary buy-back of the most flood-prone homes. Residents, the council and insurers hold different views on which option is best. The Pellow Creek township and its options are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Outline the impacts of the hypothetical Pellow Creek flash flood on people and communities, and on the natural processes of the catchment.
markerNotes: Outline asks for the main points in brief structured form. Give one impact on people and one change to the natural processes, each with a supporting detail.
Link the two sides where you can: a change to runoff in the catchment is one reason the impact on homes is greater.
commonStudentErrors: Describing only the impacts on people and forgetting the change to natural processes.
Writing a full paragraph of explanation when the question asks for an outline.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines at least one impact on people and communities and at least one change to natural processes in the catchment, with a brief supporting detail for each
2 marks: Outlines one impact, on either people and communities or natural processes, with a supporting detail
1 mark: Names an impact without outline

sampleAnswers.answer: The Pellow Creek flash flood impacts people and communities through damage to homes and roads, and through short warning times that leave residents in the lower township exposed. It also impacts natural processes in the catchment: clearing and paving increase runoff, which speeds the rise of the creek and increases erosion in the channel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines an impact on people and communities (damage and short warning times) and a change to natural processes in the catchment (faster runoff and erosion), each with a supporting detail. This is the 3-mark outline the question asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flood damages homes and roads in the township, which is an impact on people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one impact on people with a supporting detail, but no change to natural processes is included, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The flood is bad for people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names an impact without any outline or supporting detail, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: The effectiveness of people and organisations in managing ONE contemporary hazard event at a selected place

prompts.question: Evaluate the effectiveness of people and organisations in managing one flash flood event at the selected place in Pellow Creek, using clearly stated criteria.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs an explicit yardstick. State the criteria first, then judge each response against each criterion and say which it meets, partly meets or fails.
A top answer separates what the evidence shows from what residents report, and names what a fuller evaluation would need.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the warnings, drains and drill without making any judgement of effectiveness.
Judging the response on a single criterion, such as cost, and claiming an overall result.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Evaluates the effectiveness of people and organisations in managing the event against explicit criteria (warning time, damage reduction, community preparedness and cost), weighs the evidence for each response, and reaches a justified overall judgement with the limits of the evidence stated
6 marks: Evaluates effectiveness against at least two explicit criteria, with evidence, and reaches a clear judgement with limited qualification
5 marks: Evaluates the effectiveness of one or two responses with evidence against one criterion, reaching a partial judgement
3-4 marks: Describes the responses and one outcome, with little judgement
2 marks: Names an organisation or response without outcomes
1 mark: Makes a general statement about emergency management

sampleAnswers.answer: At the selected place in Pellow Creek, the effectiveness of people and organisations in managing the most recent contemporary hazard event is mixed, and the judgement depends on the criteria used. The first criterion is warning time. The emergency services and council issued warnings, but they arrived late at night, and residents report that the rise came faster than the message. On this criterion the response is only partly effective, because the warning system did its job technically but did not give enough time to act. The second criterion is damage reduction. Drains were not cleared before the storm, which increased ponding in the lower streets, so the response was weakest where it could most easily have made a difference. The third criterion is community preparedness. The evacuation drill run by the community group improved preparedness among residents who attended, and this is a genuine success, since it gave people a practical plan they could use. The fourth criterion is cost. The response used existing services and volunteers, so its cost was low, which is an advantage in a township with a limited budget. Weighing these criteria, the response is effective in preparedness and cost, but only partly effective in warning time and damage reduction. The overall judgement is that the response reduced some harm but did not manage the hazard as well as it could have. The evidence has limits: the scenario relies on residents' reports rather than on timed records of the warnings and drain works, and a fuller evaluation would need those records before a firm conclusion is reached. Recommendations should therefore focus on earlier warnings and drain maintenance before the next storm season. The council should also publish the warning times and drain-clearing records after each event, so that the next evaluation can test whether the changes improved outcomes against each criterion, and a clear standard for drain clearing would make accountability simpler.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Sets out four explicit criteria, judges the response against each, and reaches a justified overall judgement. It separates the evidence (timed records) from residents' reports and names what a fuller evaluation would need, which is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The emergency response was partly effective. Warnings came late at night, so people had little time, and the drains were not cleared before the storm. The evacuation drill helped residents who attended. Overall the response reduced some harm but did not manage the flood well.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Judges the effectiveness of the responses with some evidence and reaches a partial judgement, but only one criterion is applied in depth and the limits of the evidence are not discussed, so it sits at 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council issued warnings for the flood.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names an organisation and a response without any outcome or judgement, so it earns the 2-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The township's emergency services, council and a community group responded to the most recent flash flood in Pellow Creek by issuing warnings, clearing drains and running an evacuation drill. Residents report that the warnings arrived late at night and that the drains were not cleared before the storm. The Pellow Creek response and event are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Propose an action that would reduce the risk from future flash floods in Pellow Creek, and predict its likely outcome.
markerNotes: A proposal names an action and the mechanism by which it works. The predicted outcome should follow from that mechanism, not just be asserted.
The constraint point is what makes a proposal credible: a warning system only helps if residents act on it.
commonStudentErrors: Proposing an action with no mechanism, such as 'the council should help', and then predicting that the risk will fall.
Predicting an outcome that is certain, with no acknowledgement of constraints.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Proposes a specific, feasible action with a clear mechanism for reducing risk, predicts its likely outcome with a reason, and notes one constraint or uncertainty
3 marks: Proposes a specific action and predicts its outcome without a reason
2 marks: Proposes a general action without a predicted outcome
1 mark: Makes a general statement about reducing risk

sampleAnswers.answer: The proposed action is a warning system for Pellow Creek, linked to rain gauges in the upper catchment, so that intense bursts of rain trigger alerts before a flash flood reaches the lower township. The mechanism is time: the gauges detect the rain early, so residents have time to move vehicles and possessions. The predicted outcome is a reduction in risk to people and property in the lower valley. The main constraint is that a warning only reduces risk if residents act on it, so the limited budget must also fund clear messages and drills.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Proposes a specific action with a clear mechanism (earlier warning from rain gauges), predicts its outcome with a reason, and names the main constraint (residents must act on warnings, within a limited budget). That makes the proposal specific and credible.

sampleAnswers.answer: The council could install a warning system that gives residents more time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Proposes a general action with no mechanism and no predicted outcome, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Better drainage would help.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about reducing risk with no specific action or outcome, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The council has a limited budget for the Pellow Creek township and is choosing between a warning system linked to rain gauges and a drainage upgrade for the lower streets. The Pellow Creek township and both options are hypothetical.

dotPoints.description: Spatial and temporal characteristics of climate change at a global scale

prompts.question: Describe the spatial and temporal characteristics of climate change at a global scale, using the global temperature map and time series supplied for this question.
markerNotes: Spatial means where the change is and how it varies between places. Temporal means when it happens and how fast. Describe both, using the supplied map and time series.
A single global average hides regional variation, so an answer that notes the pattern across the globe scores higher than one that quotes a single figure.
commonStudentErrors: Describing climate change as uniform across the globe, which the map contradicts.
Quoting a time trend without saying when the rate of change accelerated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the spatial pattern of climate change at a global scale (where warming is strongest and weakest, using the map) and its temporal characteristics (the timing and rate of change, using the time series), with a supporting feature for each
3 marks: Describes either the spatial or the temporal characteristics, with a supporting feature
2 marks: Names one spatial or temporal characteristic without description
1 mark: Makes a general statement that the climate is warming

sampleAnswers.answer: The spatial characteristics of climate change at a global scale show warming that is not uniform: the hypothetical temperature map shows the strongest warming over high northern latitudes and a weaker signal over the southern oceans. The temporal characteristics show an upward trend in the time series from 1900, with a steeper rise after 1980, so the rate of change has accelerated in recent decades. Describing both dimensions shows that climate change is a global process whose place and timing both vary, so a single global average can hide important variation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the spatial pattern from the map (strongest and weakest warming) and the temporal pattern from the time series (long trend, accelerating after 1980), with supporting features. The closing point about averages hiding variation shows understanding of the scale.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change has a spatial pattern that varies across the world.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a spatial characteristic without describing where warming is strongest or weakest, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The climate is warming.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no reference to the map or the time series, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical global temperature map for one recent decade shows warming strongest over high northern latitudes and weaker over the southern oceans. A hypothetical time series from 1900 to the present shows an upward trend with a steeper rise after 1980. Both are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Recall two indicators, other than temperature, that show long-term climate change at a global scale.
markerNotes: An indicator is a measurable sign of change. Name the indicator and say what it shows, so the marker can see the link to climate change.
The question excludes temperature, so naming it earns no credit.
commonStudentErrors: Naming temperature, which the question excludes.
Naming an indicator without saying what it shows, for example writing only 'sea level'.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Names two distinct indicators of climate change at a global scale (for example sea level rise, ice sheet and glacier mass loss, or ocean heat content) and states what each shows
1 mark: Names one indicator correctly, or names temperature only

sampleAnswers.answer: Two indicators of climate change at a global scale, other than temperature, are sea level rise and glacier mass loss. Sea level rise shows ocean expansion and melting land ice, while glacier mass loss records net ice loss.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two distinct indicators, other than temperature, and states what each shows about climate change at a global scale. Both parts of the 2-mark band are met.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sea level rise is one indicator that shows climate change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one correct indicator with a brief link to climate change, but gives no second indicator, so it earns the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: Environmental and human impacts of climate change at a range of scales

prompts.question: Explain how climate change impacts natural systems, and people and communities, at a range of scales in the hypothetical Calder Delta.
markerNotes: Follow the causal chain: physical change, then the change to natural systems, then the consequence for people. Top answers name the scale of each step.
Impacts on people are not the same as the physical change. Explain how the environmental change reaches communities through a specific livelihood or hazard.
commonStudentErrors: Listing sea level rise and storm surge as impacts without saying what they do to natural systems or people.
Describing impacts at only one scale, usually the local one.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Explains how climate change impacts natural systems and people and communities at several scales, linking the physical change (sea level or storm surge) to specific environmental and human consequences in the Calder Delta, with a clear causal chain
4 marks: Explains impacts on natural systems and on people and communities at one or two scales, with a causal link for at least one
3 marks: Identifies impacts on natural systems or on people with limited explanation
2 marks: Names one impact without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement that climate change is harmful

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change impacts the Calder Delta through rising sea level and more frequent storm surges, and these impacts operate across a range of scales. Higher sea level and more frequent surges push saltwater further inland, changing the delta's natural systems, including the saltwater wetland along its edge. At the local scale, saline water reaching rice paddies reduces the yields that farmers depend on, and fishing villages are affected as the coastal waters they rely on change, so livelihoods are tied directly to the delta's natural systems. At the regional scale, more frequent storm surges expose more of the delta's settlements to flooding. Impacts on people and communities therefore follow directly from the physical change, through the changed natural systems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Traces the chain from sea level and storm surge through natural systems to people and communities, and names the scale of consequences from local to regional. The explicit causal chain is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Sea level rise lets salt water reach wetlands, which changes natural systems. People in fishing villages then lose catch and rice paddies face saltwater, so climate change impacts people as well.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies impacts on natural systems and on people, with a causal link, but the scales are not named and the explanation is limited, so it sits at 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change makes the delta flood more.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement that climate change is harmful, with no natural system or community named, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The hypothetical Calder Delta is a low-lying river delta where sea level is rising and storm surges are becoming more frequent. Rice paddies, fishing villages and a saltwater wetland line the delta's edge. The delta and its records are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Contrast the environmental impacts of climate change with the human impacts on the hypothetical Calder Delta, showing how the two differ in their timing and reversibility.
markerNotes: Contrast requires the two sides to be compared on the same criteria. Name the criterion, then show how the two impacts differ on it.
Reversibility is a useful criterion: some wetland change can be partly reversed, while land lost to the sea cannot.
commonStudentErrors: Describing environmental impacts and then human impacts in two separate paragraphs, without comparing them.
Treating all environmental impacts as irreversible, with no example.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Contrasts environmental and human impacts clearly, identifying a difference in timing and a difference in reversibility, with a specific example from the Calder Delta for each
3 marks: Contrasts the two types of impact with a difference in timing or reversibility, with a relevant example
2 marks: Describes environmental and human impacts separately, without contrasting them
1 mark: Names one impact of climate change without reference to the other type

sampleAnswers.answer: The two impacts differ in timing and reversibility. Environmental impacts of climate change on the Calder Delta, such as the saltwater wetland changing as sea level rises, tend to be gradual and cumulative. Human impacts, such as storm surges reaching fishing villages and damaging rice paddies, are often sudden and visible, because a single surge can cause damage within hours. The two also differ in reversibility: some wetland change can be partly reversed if conditions are restored, whereas land lost to the sea cannot be recovered. Human impacts can be reduced by flood protection for villages at the local scale, but lost livelihoods are harder to reverse.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Contrasts the two types on timing (gradual versus sudden) and on reversibility, with a specific example from the Calder Delta for each side.

sampleAnswers.answer: Environmental impacts include saltwater intrusion into wetlands and mangrove retreat. Human impacts include house flooding and lost rice yields.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the two types of impact separately with examples, but does not contrast them on any criterion, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change damages wetlands.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one impact without reference to the human impacts, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: Challenges, opportunities and responses

prompts.question: Justify the balance between mitigation and adaptation as responses to climate change in the Calder Delta, considering the rate and magnitude of change and the varying perspectives of governments and communities.
markerNotes: Justify means arguing for a position with reasons that can be tested. A balanced answer that still reaches a clear judgement scores more highly than a description of both responses.
The best answers show that mitigation changes the rate and magnitude of the problem, while adaptation deals with the impacts that are already committed.
commonStudentErrors: Describing mitigation and adaptation without taking a position on the balance between them.
Presenting mitigation as the only real solution, with no reference to impacts already under way.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Justifies a balance between mitigation and adaptation with evidence on the rate and magnitude of change, weighs the varying perspectives of governments and communities, explains the limits of each response, and reaches a reasoned judgement about the combination that is most defensible
5-6 marks: Justifies a balance between mitigation and adaptation with relevant reasons, considers at least one perspective and one limit of either response, but reaches only a limited judgement
4 marks: Describes mitigation and adaptation with a reasoned link to the rate of change, with limited consideration of perspectives and no clear judgement
2-3 marks: Describes the two responses in general terms with little justification, or names mitigation or adaptation with a single example
1 mark: Makes a general statement about climate change responses

sampleAnswers.answer: The balance between mitigation and adaptation for the Calder Delta depends on the rate and magnitude of change that the delta is expected to face, and a justified response must combine both. Mitigation reduces the rate and magnitude of climate change by cutting emissions at source, and its benefits are global and long-term: a large emissions reduction slows sea-level rise and limits the scale of storm intensification, which matters greatly for a low-lying delta. However, mitigation cannot prevent change that has already begun, because the ocean and ice respond slowly, so some sea-level rise is already committed. This is why adaptation is necessary. Seawalls, mangrove restoration and house raising reduce risk now, and they can be delivered at local and regional scales with immediate benefits to residents. Adaptation alone, however, is a weaker response, because the costs of defending a shoreline are likely to rise as sea-level rise accelerates, and a seawall can shift erosion to neighbouring areas. The varying perspectives of governments and communities shape the balance. Local communities favour adaptation because they can see the works and its effect on their homes, while the state argues that mitigation is needed to slow the rate of change so that adaptation remains affordable. Each perspective is partly right, but neither of these responses addresses the whole problem. The resilience of the delta depends on pursuing both responses together: mitigation keeps the magnitude of change within a range that adaptation can manage, and adaptation buys time and protection for communities while mitigation takes effect. Judged against cost, effectiveness and equity, a combined strategy is the most defensible, provided that the adaptation projects are designed to remain effective at higher levels of sea-level rise and that the funding for both is shared fairly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Argues for a combined balance, using the rate and magnitude of change to show why mitigation alone is not enough and adaptation alone is weaker. The varying perspectives are weighed, and the conclusion rests on named criteria (cost, effectiveness, equity). That reasoned judgement is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mitigation reduces the rate of climate change by cutting emissions, but it cannot stop change that is already under way. Adaptation such as seawalls and house raising reduces local risk now. Governments and communities disagree on priorities. A combined approach is probably best because it deals with both the cause and the impacts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both responses and links mitigation to the rate of change, and reaches a provisional conclusion. The perspectives are only mentioned and the limits of each response are not developed, so it sits at 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mitigation includes cutting emissions in the delta.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names mitigation with one example and no justification, so it earns the 2-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The Calder Delta's regional government is weighing a large emissions-reduction program against seawalls, mangrove restoration and house-raising schemes. Local communities favour adaptation projects they can see working, while the state argues that mitigation is needed to slow the rate of change. The Calder Delta, its government and its communities are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Differentiate between mitigation and adaptation as responses to climate change in the hypothetical Calder Delta, using one example of each.
markerNotes: Differentiate asks for the difference, so organise the answer around two or three criteria (target, scale, timing) rather than describing each response separately.
A good example names the delta and the action, such as house raising above recent flood levels, rather than a generic example.
commonStudentErrors: Describing mitigation and adaptation without showing what separates them.
Using adaptation as a synonym for any response, including reducing emissions.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Differentiates mitigation (reducing the rate and magnitude of change through emissions reduction) from adaptation (adjusting to impacts, such as raising houses), with one correct example of each applied to the Calder Delta
3 marks: Differentiates the two with a correct general explanation and one example
2 marks: Describes mitigation or adaptation without contrasting them
1 mark: Names a response without explanation

sampleAnswers.answer: Mitigation and adaptation differ as responses in the Calder Delta. Mitigation acts on the cause by reducing the rate and magnitude of change through cuts in greenhouse gas emissions, such as a renewable energy program that lowers emissions from the electricity supplying the delta. Its benefits are global and long-term, but its effect on the delta is delayed. Adaptation acts on the impacts by adjusting to change already under way, such as raising homes in the delta above the flood level of recent storm surges. Its benefits are local and immediate, but it does not address the cause. The two therefore differ in target, scale and timing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Differentiates the two on target (cause versus impacts), scale (global versus local) and timing (delayed versus immediate), with one correct example of each in the Calder Delta.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mitigation means cutting emissions to slow climate change. Adaptation is the building of seawalls in the delta.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes each response separately, with a basic example for adaptation, but does not contrast them, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mitigation is a response to climate change.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names one response without explanation or contrast, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: The effectiveness of people and organisations in managing ONE climate change challenge at a selected place

prompts.question: Assess the effectiveness of people and organisations in managing one climate change challenge at a selected place, such as the Calder Delta seawall project.
markerNotes: Assess asks for a weighed judgement. Name the criteria, show the evidence for each, and say which outcome matters most for the challenge.
Top answers are careful about the evidence: a seawall that worked in some storms is not proof that it worked in all of them.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the seawall and the replanting without judging whether they are effective.
Judging effectiveness on construction, such as the length of the wall, rather than on outcomes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of the people and organisations involved against explicit criteria (flood reduction, environmental outcomes, community acceptance), weighs the evidence for each, and reaches a clear judgement with the limits of the evidence stated
5 marks: Assesses effectiveness against at least two criteria with evidence, reaching a judgement with limited qualification
4 marks: Describes the project and its outcomes, with a comment on effectiveness but no stated criteria
3 marks: Describes the project and one outcome, with little judgement
2 marks: Names an organisation or project without outcomes
1 mark: Makes a general statement about climate change responses

sampleAnswers.answer: The effectiveness of the Calder Delta seawall and mangrove project in managing this climate change challenge at the selected place is partial, and the judgement depends on the criteria applied. On flood reduction, the seawall has reduced damage in the storm years it was designed for, so the council's stated criterion is met in those years. However, storm surge flooding still occurs in years when the surge exceeds the wall's height, so the effect is not consistent across all events. On environmental outcomes, the replanting shows mixed success: mangroves establish well at some sites that have freshwater flows, but fail at others where salinity remains too high, so the environmental criterion is met only in part. On community acceptance, residents value the protection but report that the seawall has changed local access to the foreshore. The people and organisations involved, including the council and the community group, have been effective at building the works but less effective at ensuring that the environmental benefits are achieved everywhere. The judgement is that the project is a partial success that should be adjusted by selecting replanting sites with sufficient freshwater flow. The evidence has limits, since the scenario's records do not cover a full run of storm years, so the assessment should be reviewed once more data are available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses the project against three explicit criteria, weighs the evidence for each, and reaches a judgement of partial success with a specific adjustment. The limits of the evidence are stated, which is the top-band requirement.

sampleAnswers.answer: The seawall has reduced damage in some storms but not all, and the mangrove replanting has been successful at some sites only. Residents like the protection but the foreshore has changed. Overall the project is partly effective.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes outcomes and comments on effectiveness, but the criteria are not stated, so it sits at 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Climate change responses are important.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement with no project or outcome named, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: The Calder Delta council built a seawall in the last decade and runs a mangrove replanting project on the delta's edge. Storm surge flooding has been reduced in some years but not others, and replanting success varies between sites. The Calder Delta, its projects and its records are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Clarify what is meant by a selected place for a climate change challenge, and explain why its boundaries should be set before the effectiveness of a project is assessed.
markerNotes: Clarify means making a term clear. Define the term, then show why it matters for the question.
The reason for fixing boundaries in advance is that outcomes can only be compared over the same geographic extent.
commonStudentErrors: Defining a selected place as any location, with no reference to the challenge being studied.
Setting boundaries after the results are known, which makes the assessment unreliable.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Clarifies that a selected place is a defined location at a named scale in which the challenge is studied, explains why its boundaries must be fixed before assessing effectiveness (so outcomes are measured over the same area), and gives one example of a boundary decision
2 marks: Clarifies the meaning of a selected place, with one reason for setting its boundaries
1 mark: Gives a general definition of a place without reference to effectiveness

sampleAnswers.answer: A selected place is a defined location, at a named scale, within which a climate change challenge is studied. Its boundaries must be fixed before the effectiveness of a project is assessed, so that outcomes are measured over the same geographic extent. For example, the selected place might be the lower township and its adjacent wetland rather than the whole Calder Delta.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies the term (defined location, named scale, challenge studied), gives an example of a boundary decision, and explains why boundaries must be fixed in advance so outcomes are comparable.

sampleAnswers.answer: A selected place is an area where the climate change challenge is studied, and its boundaries should be fixed so that the project can be judged on the same area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Clarifies the meaning and gives one reason for fixing the boundaries, but no example of a boundary decision, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: A selected place is a location.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general definition with no link to the challenge or to effectiveness, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

subTopics.name: In learning about geographical inquiry in the contemporary world, students investigate:

dotPoints.description: The nature of geographical inquiry and how it can contribute to the understanding and effective management of places and environments

prompts.question: Discuss the nature of geographical inquiry and how it can contribute to understanding and effective management of places and environments, using a local flood problem as your example.
markerNotes: Discuss means arguing both the strengths and the limits of inquiry. A description of the inquiry process alone sits in the lower bands.
Top answers show how the flood example illustrates the contribution, for instance how a levee changes runoff and so changes what the inquiry must measure.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the steps of an inquiry without saying how they contribute to understanding or management.
Treating inquiry as producing certain answers, with no acknowledgement of data limits.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Discusses the nature of geographical inquiry (evidence-based, systematic, open to testing) and explains with specific reasons how it contributes to understanding and to effective management, weighs its limits, and uses the flood example to support a reasoned conclusion
5-6 marks: Discusses the nature of inquiry and at least one way it contributes to understanding or management, with some reference to the flood example
4 marks: Describes inquiry and its contribution in general terms, with some links between them
2-3 marks: Lists features of inquiry or uses of evidence without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about geography or flooding

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry is a systematic process of asking geographical questions, collecting evidence about places and environments, analysing that evidence and communicating conclusions. Its nature is that it is evidence-based and open to testing: a claim about flood risk must be supported by data, and the method must be transparent enough for others to check it. This nature allows inquiry to contribute to understanding in several ways. First, it separates what is known from what is assumed, so that a council considering a levee can see which parts of its case rest on measured rainfall and which rest on expectation. Second, it reveals the interactions among the physical processes, human decisions and place characteristics that shape a problem, which a single observation cannot show. A levee changes runoff, sediment and the flood extent downstream, and an inquiry that follows these links produces a more complete understanding than a simple cost comparison. Third, inquiry contributes to effective management because it allows options to be compared against criteria and monitored afterwards. Management is more effective when the outcomes of a decision are measured, so that a warning system or a levee can be judged and adjusted. However, the contribution of inquiry has limits. Findings depend on the quality of data and the choice of questions, and results may be contested by groups with different interests, so the inquiry must be communicated openly. The most useful inquiries therefore combine rigorous method with clear communication, so that the understanding they produce can inform decisions about places and environments. Overall, inquiry contributes to understanding and effective management by making decisions about places and environments more evidence-based, transparent and reviewable. For the council in the township, this means the levee decision can be revisited if monitored results show that the expected reduction in flood extent is not being achieved, which is itself a benefit of inquiry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines the nature of inquiry (evidence-based, testable), explains three specific contributions (understanding, system interactions, management), uses the levee example throughout, and weighs the limits. The reasoned conclusion is the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry asks questions and collects evidence about places. It helps understanding because it shows the links between rainfall, runoff and flooding. It also helps management because options can be compared. But results depend on data quality, so the council should not treat any single inquiry as final.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses the nature of inquiry and two contributions with some reference to the flood example, and notes one limit. The contribution is not developed in depth, so it sits in the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry uses evidence and maps. It is done by students.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Lists features of inquiry without any explanation of how it contributes to understanding or management, so it falls in the 2-3 band.

prompts.scenario: A Year 11 class is investigating whether a proposed flood levee would reduce risk in a hypothetical township. They must decide what their inquiry can and cannot tell the council before the decision is made. The township and proposal are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Define geographical inquiry, explain how it differs from a general news report about a place, and give one example of a question an inquiry could answer.
markerNotes: A definition needs the method as well as the subject. Saying that an inquiry is about places is not enough without the evidence and method.
A good example question is specific, measurable and tied to a place, which shows the student can apply the definition.
commonStudentErrors: Defining geographical inquiry as simply researching a topic, with no reference to method or evidence.
Giving an example question that cannot be answered with evidence, such as whether a place is beautiful.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines geographical inquiry as a systematic, evidence-based process of asking questions about places and environments, distinguishes it from a general report by its method and evidence, and gives one valid example question
2 marks: Defines geographical inquiry, with one distinguishing feature or one example
1 mark: Gives a general definition of inquiry without reference to places or methods

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry is a systematic, evidence-based process of investigating a question about places and environments. It differs from a general news report because it follows a stated method, makes its evidence transparent and tests its conclusions. An example question is whether a flood levee has reduced flooding in the township, which can be tested with flood records before and after construction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines the inquiry with its method and evidence, distinguishes it from a news report by method and testing, and gives a specific, testable example question tied to a place.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry is an investigation of a place using evidence. An example question is whether a levee reduces flooding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines inquiry and gives one example question, but does not distinguish it from a general report, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Geographical inquiry is studying places.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general definition with no reference to method or evidence, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: The nature of engagement with geographical opportunities and challenges in the public sphere, including the role and influence of research institutions, government, advocacy groups, the media and the individual

prompts.question: Explain how research institutions, government, advocacy groups, the media and individuals engage with geographical opportunities and challenges in the public sphere, and how their relative influence varies.
markerNotes: Explain the mechanism of engagement for each group, such as evidence, funding and approval, or framing and amplification. Naming the group is not enough.
The variation in influence is the top-band point: research shapes the technical evidence early, while government makes the final decision.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the five groups with one sentence each and no comment on influence.
Treating the media as neutral reporting, with no account of how it frames the debate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains how each of the five groups (research institutions, government, advocacy groups, the media and individuals) engages with a geographical opportunity or challenge in the public sphere, and evaluates how their relative influence varies with evidence and scale
5 marks: Explains the engagement of at least four groups, with a clear account of their influence on the outcome
4 marks: Explains the roles of three groups in the public sphere, with limited comment on influence
3 marks: Identifies two or three groups and their roles, with little explanation
2 marks: Names a group and its role without explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about public debate

sampleAnswers.answer: Research institutions, government, advocacy groups, the media and individuals engage with the levee proposal in the public sphere, but their influence differs. The university hydrology group shapes the technical evidence, showing how a levee would change flood extent, so its influence is strongest early in the debate. Government holds the power to fund and approve the levee, making it decisive on the outcome, though it is constrained by budgets and the evidence it receives. Advocacy groups, such as the residents' group, can shift government priorities by mobilising public support. The media, here a local newspaper, frames the debate and shapes how the risk is perceived rather than the formal decision. Individuals influence the outcome through submissions, and a well-argued submission can add local knowledge that other groups lack. The variation reflects the stage and scale of the debate: research shapes the evidence, advocacy and the media shape the public stage, and government makes the final decision.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the mechanism of engagement for each of the five groups in the levee scenario and evaluates how their influence varies by stage (technical evidence, public stage, final decision). The closing point on stage and scale is what makes the answer evaluative, as the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: Research institutions provide evidence about flood risk, and government makes the final decision. Advocacy groups represent residents and conservationists, and the media reports the debate. Individuals can make submissions to the council.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the roles of several groups in the public sphere, but the comment on how influence varies is limited, so it sits at 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Many people and groups have views about floods.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement about public debate with no group's engagement explained, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A hypothetical proposal to build a flood levee in a township has drawn responses from a university hydrology group, the state government, a residents' advocacy group, a local newspaper and individual residents. The proposal and its participants are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Outline the roles of the media and of individual residents in shaping the public response to a flood levee proposal, and the challenges this creates for the council.
markerNotes: Outline is brief but structured. Give each role, its mechanism and one effect on the proposal, rather than a general description of public debate.
A challenge for the council is the link that lifts the answer above a list of two roles.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the media as a single block, with no mechanism for how it shapes the response.
Writing about residents' views without saying how their actions change the proposal.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the role of the media (reporting, framing and amplifying views) and of individual residents (submissions, petitions and votes) in shaping the public response, with one specific effect on the proposal for each, and one challenge for the council
3 marks: Outlines both roles with one effect identified
2 marks: Outlines one role with a supporting detail
1 mark: Names one role without outline

sampleAnswers.answer: The roles of the media and individual residents in shaping the public response are distinct. The media decides which views reach the public and how risk is framed. Reporting that emphasises flood frequency can build support for the flood levee, while coverage of its cost can strengthen opposition. Individual residents shape the response through submissions, petitions and votes, and many submissions can prompt the council to change the proposal, such as by adding a warning system. The challenges for the council are that the media and individuals may push the proposal in different directions, so it must weigh a loud public response against the technical evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the media's mechanism (framing what reaches the public) and the residents' mechanism (submissions, petitions, votes), each with an effect on the proposal, and states a challenge for the council. This matches the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The media reports on the levee and can make people support or oppose it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines one role with a supporting detail but does not address individual residents or a challenge for the council, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Individuals can take part in debates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a role without outline or any effect on the proposal, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

subTopics.name: In undertaking the Geographical Investigation, students:

dotPoints.description: Identify an area for geographical inquiry

prompts.question: Apply three criteria to identify an area for geographical inquiry within the hypothetical Pellow Creek catchment, and state which area the student should select.
markerNotes: Apply means using the criteria on the candidate areas, not just listing them. Each criterion should produce a comparison between the areas.
State the choice explicitly and give the main reason; a balanced note on the rejected areas can add value.
commonStudentErrors: Listing criteria such as 'interesting' or 'easy' that are not tied to the inquiry question or the scenario.
Choosing an area without applying the criteria to each candidate.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Applies three clear criteria (for example relevance to the inquiry question, data availability, and safety or access) to the candidate areas, and identifies the area that best meets them, with a reason
3 marks: Applies three criteria to the areas with a justified choice, but one criterion is not clearly applied
2 marks: Names two relevant criteria and applies them to the areas, without a clear choice
1 mark: Names one criterion or a general aim without applying it

sampleAnswers.answer: Applying three criteria to the Pellow Creek candidate areas favours the lower valley near the township. Relevance: the lower valley is where flood impacts on people are most direct, so an inquiry there addresses a question that matters to residents and the council. Data: the township's proximity suggests local records may be easier to obtain. Safety and access: the upper slopes are steep and may be unsafe during intense storms, whereas the lower valley can be visited more safely. The student should therefore select the lower valley as the area for geographical inquiry, while noting that the upper slopes remain relevant to the cause.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies relevance, data and safety/access to the candidate areas, states a clear choice with a reason, and notes what the rejected upper slopes still offer. The balanced judgement is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The lower valley is the best area because it has flood records and is close to the township. The upper slopes are not safe in storms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two relevant criteria and applies them to the areas, and makes a choice, but the reasoning for the choice is not set out against three criteria, so it sits at 2 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should choose an area that is easy to study.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a general aim without applying any criterion to the candidate areas, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A Year 11 class has three candidate areas in the hypothetical Pellow Creek catchment: the upper slopes with thin soil, the lower valley near the township, and an estuary access road. Each area has different relevance, data, access and safety conditions. The candidate areas are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Define an area for geographical inquiry, and state one criterion that makes an area suitable for a Year 11 investigation.
markerNotes: Give both parts. The definition covers what an area is, and the criterion shows the student can judge whether an area is worth studying.
Manageable boundaries are a practical criterion: an area too large to survey within the time available cannot support a sound investigation.
commonStudentErrors: Defining the area as a location only, with no reference to a question being investigated.
Stating a criterion that is not about suitability, such as the area being large or popular.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Defines an area for geographical inquiry as a defined location at a stated scale in which a question can be investigated, and states one criterion that makes it suitable (such as access to data or manageable boundaries)
1 mark: Gives a definition or a criterion, but not both

sampleAnswers.answer: An area for geographical inquiry is a defined location, at a stated scale, in which a question can be investigated. A suitable criterion is manageable boundaries, so the student can finish the investigation within the time available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines the area as a defined location at a stated scale in which a question can be investigated, and states a suitability criterion (manageable boundaries) with a reason. Both parts are present.

sampleAnswers.answer: An area for geographical inquiry is a place that the student studies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives a definition without a criterion for suitability, so it earns the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: Develop geographical questions and formulate a plan

prompts.question: Synthesise the decisions a student must make to develop a geographical question and formulate a plan for a flood investigation in Pellow Creek, including the focus, the geographic extent, the sequence of steps and the time allocated to each step.
markerNotes: Synthesise asks for the decisions to be combined. The top band shows that each decision is consistent with the others and with the time and resources given.
A plan with a buffer for weather or delays shows the student has thought about feasibility, which the marker looks for.
commonStudentErrors: Setting a focus that is too broad to answer in the time available.
Planning a field day before the records have been checked, so the data collected cannot answer the question.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Synthesises the focus, geographic extent, sequence and time allocation into one consistent plan, shows how each decision follows from the others and from the resources available, and justifies the plan's feasibility
6 marks: Combines at least three of the decisions into a coherent plan with relevant justification, and notes a constraint on timing or resources
5 marks: Combines some of the decisions into a plan with limited justification, and the links between focus, extent, sequence and time are only partly developed
3-4 marks: Lists or describes the decisions the plan requires, with some links between them but little justification
2 marks: Names some of the focus, extent, sequence or time, or states that a plan is needed, without linking them
1 mark: Makes a general statement about planning an investigation

sampleAnswers.answer: Developing a geographical question for a flood investigation in the Pellow Creek catchment requires the student to make four linked decisions, and synthesising them into one plan is what turns a general interest in flooding into a researchable project. The focus comes first: the question must be narrow enough to answer in ten weeks, such as whether a drainage upgrade has reduced flood depth in the lower streets, rather than whether flooding in general is a problem. The focus should also be testable with the council records and the single field day available. The geographic extent follows from the focus. If the question concerns the lower streets, the extent is the valley floor and the township, and the upper slopes are included only as the source of runoff that feeds the question. Setting the extent first prevents the investigation from spreading across the whole catchment, which would make the data collection unmanageable. The sequence of steps should then move from the records to the field. The student first gathers and checks the council flood records and the drainage plans, because these determine what can be measured. Next comes the field day, when the student records water depths and observes the drains, and last comes the analysis, in which the records and field data are compared. Sequencing the work this way means the field day is designed with the records in hand, rather than collected without a clear purpose. Time must be allocated to each stage so that the plan is achievable. A realistic allocation gives two weeks to the focus and planning, three weeks to gathering and checking records, one day to the field work with a further week for processing the data, and the remaining time to analysis and writing. Each allocation should include a buffer, because weather can cancel a field day and records may take longer to obtain than expected. Synthesising the four decisions yields a plan in which the question, extent, sequence and timing are consistent with one another, and that consistency is what makes the investigation credible to the council and to the examiner.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Combines the focus, geographic extent, sequence and time allocation into one plan where each decision follows from the others. The buffer for weather and records shows the plan is feasible, which is what the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should choose a focus, such as the effect of drains on flood depth, and set the extent to the lower streets. The steps should go from records to fieldwork to analysis, with time allocated to each. A buffer is needed in case the field day is cancelled by weather.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Combines the focus, extent, sequence and timing into a coherent plan, and notes a constraint on timing. The justification is brief and the links are not fully developed, so it sits at 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student needs a geographical question and a plan for the Pellow Creek investigation.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that a question and plan are needed without listing the focus, extent, sequence or time, so it earns the 2-mark level.

prompts.scenario: A Year 11 student has chosen the Pellow Creek catchment for a flood investigation but has not yet decided its focus. The student has ten weeks, access to council flood records and one field day. The Pellow Creek catchment, the student and the constraints are hypothetical.

prompts.question: Outline the questions a student should ask about the focus and geographic extent of a hypothetical Pellow Creek flood investigation.
markerNotes: Outline asks for the main questions in brief structured form. Each question should be one that must be answered before data is collected.
The focus question and the extent question are the two most important, because the rest of the plan depends on them.
commonStudentErrors: Asking questions about the findings, which come at the end, rather than the planning questions the task asks for.
Stating questions with no purpose, so the marker cannot see why each one matters.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines three questions (the focus of the research, the geographic extent, and the sequence and time for each step), each with its purpose for the investigation
2 marks: Outlines two questions with their purpose
1 mark: Names a question without outline

sampleAnswers.answer: The focus question asks what the Pellow Creek investigation will examine, which defines the problem for every later step. The geographic extent question asks which streets, catchment area or channel reach the investigation covers, which sets the area for data collection. The sequence and time question asks how each step is ordered and timed, so that the investigation stays within the time available.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines three planning questions (focus, geographic extent, sequence and time), each with its purpose for the investigation. This is the full 3-mark outline.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should ask what the focus is and what the geographic extent is.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names two planning questions without explaining why each matters, so it earns the 2-mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The student should ask a question about flooding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a general question without outline or purpose, so it earns only the 1-mark level.

dotPoints.description: Identify and observe relevant ethical practices when conducting the investigation

prompts.question: Discuss the ethical practices a student must observe when collecting flood-impact data from residents of Pellow Creek, including consent, privacy and the risk of harm.
markerNotes: Ethical practice in geographical inquiry covers the people in the study as well as the data. The top band applies each practice to a specific part of the scenario.
Show how the practice would be observed, such as a signed consent form or anonymised records. A practice without a method stays in the middle band.
commonStudentErrors: Listing ethical principles without applying them to the residents or the photographs in the scenario.
Overlooking physical risk, such as recording water levels in floodwater.
prompts.markingCriteria:
