sampleAnswers.feedback: States a view without a calculation, so it earns the 1 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical pie graphs of household energy use in two suburbs, not real data. Pie 1 (diameter 4 cm) represents 800 households, and its solar panel segment measures 90 degrees. Pie 2 (diameter 5 cm) represents 1,200 households, and its solar panel segment measures 60 degrees.

dotPoints.description: Interpret frequency distributions and diagrams

prompts.question: Interpret the frequency distribution of daily commuting distances for the 40 workers in the hypothetical suburb, identifying the modal class and the proportion of workers who travel under 10 kilometres.
markerNotes: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, not the class with the highest distance. Read the frequency column, not the class labels.
The proportion is calculated against the total number of workers (40), and adding the classes below 10 kilometres gives the numerator.
commonStudentErrors: Naming the class with the highest distance, or the widest class, rather than the class with the highest frequency.
Calculating the proportion from one class only, rather than adding the two classes below 10 kilometres.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Identifies the modal class as 5 to 9 km (14 workers), calculates that 20 of 40 workers (50 per cent) travel under 10 km, and interprets the spread of the distribution, noting that most workers commute between 5 and 14 km
3 marks: Identifies the modal class and calculates the proportion correctly, without interpreting the spread
2 marks: Identifies the modal class correctly, or calculates the proportion correctly, but not both
1 mark: States that the distribution is shown in classes with frequencies, without identifying the modal class or the proportion

sampleAnswers.answer: Interpreting the frequency distribution of commuting distances, the modal class is 5 to 9 kilometres, with 14 workers, the tallest class and so the most common distance. The proportion of workers who travel under 10 kilometres is found by adding the first two classes: 6 + 14 = 20 workers, or 20 ÷ 40 = 50 per cent. Most workers therefore commute between 5 and 14 kilometres, with 12 in the 10 to 14 kilometre class. Only 8 workers, one fifth of the total, travel 15 kilometres or more, so long commutes are less common in this suburb. The distribution is clustered in the middle classes, so the typical commute is moderate rather than long.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the modal class, calculates the proportion under 10 km, and interprets the spread of the distribution with figures. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The modal class is 5 to 9 kilometres, and half of the 40 workers, or 20, travel under 10 kilometres.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The modal class and the proportion are both correct, without interpretation of the spread, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The modal class is 5 to 9 kilometres with 14 workers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the modal class correctly but does not calculate the proportion, so it earns the 2 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical frequency distribution, not real data. Daily one-way commuting distances, rounded to the nearest kilometre, for 40 workers are: 0 to 4 km, 6 workers; 5 to 9 km, 14 workers; 10 to 14 km, 12 workers; 15 to 19 km, 5 workers; 20 km or more, 3 workers.

prompts.question: Interpret the frequency distribution of litter items counted in 20 quadrats, identifying the modal class, describing the shape of the distribution and explaining what the shape suggests about the litter at the site.
markerNotes: Describe the shape by its peaks and tails. A single peak with tails of similar size is roughly symmetrical.
Link the shape to the litter. A symmetrical shape suggests that typical counts cluster around the middle, not that a few extreme quadrats dominate.
commonStudentErrors: Confusing the modal class with the class that has the largest litter count, rather than the class with the most quadrats.
Describing the shape without linking it to what it suggests about the litter at the site.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Identifies the modal class as 10 to 14 items (7 quadrats), describes the shape as roughly symmetrical with a single peak, and explains what this suggests about the litter (typical counts clustered around the middle rather than a few heavily littered quadrats), using the quadrat counts
4 marks: Identifies the modal class and describes the shape, with an explanation that is only partly developed
3 marks: Identifies the modal class with figures and describes the shape, without interpreting it
2 marks: Identifies the modal class, without describing the shape
1 mark: States that the data are shown as classes with frequencies, without identifying the modal class

sampleAnswers.answer: The frequency distribution has its modal class at 10 to 14 litter items, which contains 7 of the 20 quadrats, the largest group. The shape is roughly symmetrical, with a single peak in the middle classes. The two tails are almost equal: 7 quadrats fall in the 0 to 4 and 5 to 9 classes, and 6 fall in the 15 to 19 and 20 to 24 classes. This shape suggests that most quadrats hold a similar, moderate number of litter items, so a typical quadrat holds about 10 to 14 items rather than a few heavily littered quadrats dominating the count. Because the upper tail is short, no single heavily littered quadrat is driving the result, so the typical level of litter at the site is moderate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the modal class from the quadrat counts, describes the shape with the tail sizes, and explains what the shape suggests about the litter. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The modal class is 10 to 14 litter items, with 7 quadrats, and the distribution has a single peak and is roughly symmetrical.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the modal class and describes the shape, but does not interpret what the shape suggests, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The data are shown as classes with frequencies.

dotPoints.description: Interpret and analyse population profiles

prompts.question: Interpret the population profile of Hypothetical Country X, identifying the shape of its population pyramid and explaining what the shape suggests about births, ageing and dependency.
markerNotes: Read the pyramid from the base upwards. A narrow base means fewer young people, which usually reflects lower birth rates over time.
Dependency rises when the older age groups grow relative to the working-age group, which is what the substantial upper bands suggest here.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the shape without explaining what the base or the top indicates about births and ageing.
Confusing a narrow base with a high proportion of children.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Identifies the shape (narrow base, widest middle-age bands and substantial upper bands) and explains that the narrow base indicates low birth rates and the large upper bands indicate ageing, with the dependency implication for the future
3 marks: Identifies the shape with the age structure figures, and explains either the low births or the ageing, but not the dependency implication
2 marks: Identifies the shape or the narrow base, without explaining what it indicates
1 mark: States that a population pyramid shows age and sex, without interpreting the shape

sampleAnswers.answer: Interpreting the population profile of Hypothetical Country X, its population pyramid has a narrow base, with only 12 per cent aged 0 to 14, and widest middle bands, with 66 per cent aged 15 to 64. In this hypothetical profile, the narrow base suggests low birth rates. The substantial upper bands, with 22 per cent aged 65 and over, show that the population is ageing. This ageing shape means the dependency ratio is likely to rise, because fewer young people enter the workforce to support more older residents. Planners would need to prepare for greater demand on health and retirement services.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the narrow base and the substantial upper bands with figures, explains the low births and the ageing, and draws out the dependency implication. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The pyramid has a narrow base, with 12 per cent aged 0 to 14, and 22 per cent are aged 65 and over, which shows the population is ageing. The dependency implication for the future is not discussed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the shape with figures and explains the ageing, but not the dependency implication, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: A population pyramid shows the age and sex of a population.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes what a pyramid shows without interpreting this one, so it earns the 1 mark level.

Hypothetical Country X has 12 per cent of its population aged 0 to 14 years, 66 per cent aged 15 to 64 years and 22 per cent aged 65 years and over. Males and females are roughly equal in each band. The base of the population pyramid is narrow, and the widest bands are in the middle-age groups, with substantial numbers in the upper bands.

prompts.question: Analyse the population profiles of Region P and Region Q, comparing their shapes and the challenges each population is likely to face.
markerNotes: Analysis links the shape to its consequence. A broad base means a growing number of school-age children, which creates demand for schools and housing.
Compare the profiles as a pair. The contrast between the two shapes is what makes the challenges different for each region.
commonStudentErrors: Describing both shapes without identifying a challenge for either region.
Mixing up the two regions when quoting the percentages.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses both profiles with figures, comparing the broad base of Region P (a young, growing population) with the narrow base of Region Q (low births and an ageing population), and identifies a specific challenge for each region, such as school and housing demand for P and health and retirement services for Q
5 marks: Compares both profiles with figures and identifies a challenge for each, with an explanation of one challenge only
4 marks: Describes both profiles with figures and identifies one challenge
3 marks: Describes the shape of one profile with figures, without comparison
2 marks: States that the two regions have different shapes, without figures
1 mark: Names one feature of a profile without describing it

sampleAnswers.answer: The two population profiles have opposite shapes, and this points to different challenges. Region P has a broad base, with 35 per cent of its population aged 0 to 14, which indicates high birth rates and a young, growing population. Only 4 per cent are aged 65 and over, so the top is narrow. Region Q has a narrow base, with only 13 per cent aged 0 to 14, which indicates low birth rates. Its middle is broad, with 70 per cent aged 15 to 64, and 17 per cent are aged 65 and over, so the population is ageing. The main challenge for Region P is to provide schools and housing for the large number of young people who will enter the workforce. For Region Q, as its working-age group grows older, demand for health care and retirement services is likely to increase, while fewer young people enter the workforce to support them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses both profiles with figures, sets the broad base against the narrow base, and identifies a specific challenge for each region. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Region P has a broad base and 35 per cent aged 0 to 14, while Region Q has a narrow base and 17 per cent aged 65 and over, so Region P needs schools while Region Q faces ageing.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both profiles with figures and identifies one challenge, so it earns the 4 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Region P and Region Q have different population shapes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States that the shapes differ without figures, so it earns the 2 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical population profiles, not real regions. Region P has a broad base, with 35 per cent of its population aged 0 to 14 and only 4 per cent aged 65 and over. Region Q has a narrow base, with 13 per cent aged 0 to 14, a broad middle with 70 per cent aged 15 to 64, and 17 per cent aged 65 and over.

dotPoints.description: Use scatter graphs and ternary graphs to identify correlations within data

prompts.question: Describe the correlation shown in the hypothetical scatter graph, including its direction and strength, and explain why the graph alone cannot show that one variable causes the other.
markerNotes: Describe a correlation by its direction (positive or negative) and its strength (strong, moderate or weak), using the pattern of the whole band of points rather than single points.
A scatter graph shows association, not cause. Use the word correlation, and avoid saying that distance from the car park causes the litter.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the correlation positive because the axes run from low to high.
Stating that the car park causes the litter, which goes beyond what a scatter graph can show.

4 marks: Describes the correlation as negative and strong, with reference to the scatter graph (litter per quadrat falls as distance from the car park increases), and explains that a correlation does not establish cause
3 marks: Describes the direction and strength correctly, without the explanation about cause
2 marks: Describes the direction only, or the strength only
1 mark: States that the points are plotted, without describing a correlation

sampleAnswers.answer: The scatter graph shows that the direction of the correlation is negative: litter items per quadrat fall as distance from the car park increases. The strength of the correlation is strong, because the points fall in a steep band from the top left to the bottom right, with only a few points outside it. However, a correlation does not establish cause. The graph shows that the two variables are associated, but it cannot prove that distance from the car park causes the lower counts, since other factors that vary along the reserve could also explain the pattern.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the negative and strong correlation with reference to the scatter graph and the quadrats, and explains why a correlation does not establish cause. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The correlation is negative and strong, as the points slope steeply downwards, but no explanation about cause is given.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the direction and strength correctly without the cause explanation, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The graph plots distance and litter for each quadrat.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States what is plotted without describing a correlation, so it earns the 1 mark level.

markerNotes: On a ternary graph, a point's position shows its mix of uses. The point sits closest to the corner whose share is highest.

Suburb A has the highest residential share, at 80 per cent, so its point lies closest to the residential corner. The residential share falls as the industrial share rises: Suburb A has 10 per cent industrial, Suburb C has 30 per cent, and Suburb D, with 50 per cent industrial, has only 20 per cent residential, so its point lies towards the industrial corner. dotPoints.description: Calculate absolute and proportional change

prompts.question: Calculate the absolute change and the proportional change, expressed as a percentage, in the population of the hypothetical town from 4,200 people in 2015 to 5,100 people in 2024. Show your working.
markerNotes: Absolute change is the new value minus the old value. Proportional change divides that change by the original value, not the new value.
Give the proportional change as a percentage, and state the base year clearly so that the reader knows which value was used.
commonStudentErrors: Dividing by the new value (5,100) rather than the original value (4,200), which gives 17.6 per cent.
Reporting the absolute change without its sign or units.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Calculates the absolute change as +900 people and the proportional change as 21.4 per cent against the 2015 base, with the working shown for both measures
2 marks: Calculates the absolute change correctly and attempts the proportional change, but uses the wrong base, such as the 2024 population, or gives only one of the two measures with working
1 mark: Recognises that absolute change is the difference between two population values, without calculating either measure

sampleAnswers.answer: Working. The absolute change in population is 5,100 − 4,200 = +900 people. The proportional change is the absolute change divided by the 2015 population, so 900 ÷ 4,200 × 100 = 21.4 per cent. Expressed as a percentage, the population of the hypothetical town grew by 21.4 per cent between 2015 and 2024, a change that can be compared with other towns of different sizes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States both measures, calculates the absolute change of +900 and the proportional change of 21.4 per cent against the original base, and explains the base. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The absolute change is +900 people. Dividing by the 2024 population gives 900 ÷ 5,100 × 100 = 17.6 per cent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The absolute change is correct, but the proportional change uses the wrong base, so it earns the 2 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Absolute change is the difference between the two population values.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the definition without calculating the change, so it earns the 1 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical town, not a real place. The population was 4,200 in 2015 and 5,100 in 2024.

prompts.question: Calculate the absolute change and the proportional change in the number of dwellings in Town P, and explain why proportional change is more useful than absolute change when comparing Town P with Town Q.
markerNotes: Keep the sign in both measures. A negative value shows a decrease, and the proportional change is calculated against the 2010 value.
The comparison is the key idea. A town that lost 400 dwellings may have lost a smaller share of its stock than a town that lost 240, so the proportional change is the fairer basis for comparison.
commonStudentErrors: Concluding that Town Q declined more because its absolute change is larger, without comparing the proportional change.
Calculating the proportional change against the 2020 value instead of the 2010 value.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates the absolute change in Town P as −240 dwellings and the proportional change as −16 per cent, then explains that absolute change can mislead when comparing towns of different size, using Town Q (−400 dwellings but −10 per cent) to show why proportional change is the fairer comparison
3 marks: Correct absolute and proportional change for Town P, with an explanation that is partly developed or uses no figures from Town Q
2 marks: Correct absolute change or correct proportional change for Town P, but not both, without the explanation
1 mark: States that absolute change is the simple difference and proportional change is a percentage, without calculating either for the towns

sampleAnswers.answer: Working. The absolute change in Town P is 1,260 − 1,500 = −240 dwellings. The proportional change is −240 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = −16 per cent. Absolute change can mislead when comparing towns of different size. Town Q lost 400 dwellings, a larger absolute change, but its proportional change is −400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = −10 per cent. Proportional change is the fairer basis for comparing Town P with Town Q, because each is measured against its own 2010 total, so Town P has lost a larger share of its dwellings. On absolute change alone Town Q looks worse, which is the misleading impression that proportional change corrects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates both measures for Town P and uses Town Q to show why proportional change is the fairer comparison. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Town P lost 240 dwellings, which is −16 per cent of its 2010 total. Proportional change is more useful when comparing towns of different sizes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Correct absolute and proportional change for Town P, with a general explanation but no figures from Town Q, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Absolute change is the simple difference, and proportional change is shown as a percentage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the definitions without calculating either change for the towns, so it earns the 1 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical towns, not real places. Town P had 1,500 dwellings in 2010 and 1,260 dwellings in 2020. Town Q had 4,000 dwellings in 2010 and 3,600 dwellings in 2020.

dotPoints.description: Construct, interpret and analyse tables and graphs

prompts.question: Construct a table that summarises these hypothetical raw counts, showing the weekly total for each site, the weekend total and the weekend share of each site's weekly total, rounded to one decimal place.
markerNotes: Check each total by adding the raw counts again. The weekend share is the weekend total divided by the weekly total, multiplied by 100.
State the rounding rule and the units in the headings, so that each column can be read without the raw counts.
commonStudentErrors: Leaving out units or the rounding, so readers cannot interpret the figures.
Calculating the weekend share from the weekend total of the other site.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Constructs a table with the weekly totals for each site (160 and 30 items), the weekend totals (108 and 20 items) and the weekend shares rounded to one decimal place (67.5 and 66.7 per cent), with headings and units
3 marks: Correct weekly and weekend totals, with the shares missing or one share wrong
2 marks: Correct weekly totals only, or shares calculated without the weekend totals
1 mark: States that the table should show the totals for each site, without constructing it

sampleAnswers.answer: Table of litter items by site (hypothetical). Columns: Site | Weekly total (items) | Weekend total (items) | Weekend share (%, rounded to one decimal place). Site 1 (car park): 160 | 108 | 67.5. Site 2 (bushland): 30 | 20 | 66.7. Each weekly total is the sum of the four sampling days, and each weekend share is the weekend total divided by the weekly total, multiplied by 100. The headings state the units, so each column can be read without the raw counts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Constructs a table with weekly totals, weekend totals and weekend shares rounded to one decimal place, with units in the headings. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Site 1: weekly total 160 items, weekend total 108 items. Site 2: weekly total 30 items, weekend total 20 items. The weekend shares are not given.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Correct weekly and weekend totals, with the shares missing, so it earns the 3 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: The table should show the total for each site.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States what the table should show without constructing it, so it earns the 1 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical raw counts of litter items at two sites over four sampling days, not real data. Site 1 (car park): Monday 30 items, Tuesday 22 items, Saturday 58 items, Sunday 50 items. Site 2 (bushland): Monday 6 items, Tuesday 4 items, Saturday 9 items, Sunday 11 items.

prompts.question: Analyse the trend in the hypothetical table of weekly litter items and rainfall, identifying the peak week and one limitation of using the table to establish cause.
markerNotes: Analyse the trend by stating its direction and the peak, then link the change to the other variable in the table.
A table shows association over time, so the limitation should explain why the link cannot prove cause or be generalised to other places.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each row of the table in turn without identifying a trend.
Stating that rainfall caused the fall in litter without naming a limitation.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the trend with figures (a rise to a peak of 52 items in week 3, then a fall to 25 items in week 6), links the fall in weeks 5 and 6 to the higher weekly rainfall, and identifies a specific limitation such as the short period or the single site
5 marks: Analyses the trend with figures and links it to rainfall, but the limitation is missing or unclear
4 marks: Describes the trend with figures and a link to rainfall, with little analysis of why, and names a limitation
3 marks: Describes the trend with figures, without linking it to rainfall or naming a limitation
2 marks: Describes the trend in general terms, such as litter rising and falling, without figures
1 mark: States that the table shows litter items and rainfall by week, without describing a trend

sampleAnswers.answer: The table shows a clear trend: weekly litter items rise from 35 in week 1 to a peak of 52 in week 3, then fall to 25 by week 6. The peak is the highest value in the table, marking the period of greatest litter. The decline after the peak coincides with the heaviest weekly rainfall, 18 mm in week 5 and 22 mm in week 6, compared with 0 to 5 mm in the weeks before. The pattern suggests that heavier rain may wash litter away or reduce visitor numbers, which would lower the counts. However, the table cannot show that rainfall caused the fall, since the two variables are only shown side by side, and other factors could also explain it. The main limitation is that the table covers six weeks at one site, so it shows association over a short period and cannot separate the effect of rainfall from other changes. A longer record across several sites would be needed before the trend could be generalised.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the rise to the peak and the fall with figures, links the fall to the highest weekly rainfall, and names a specific limitation about cause and period. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Litter items rise to 52 in week 3 and fall to 25 by week 6, with the heaviest rain in weeks 5 and 6, but the table cannot show that the rain caused the fall, and the record covers only six weeks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the trend with figures, links the fall to rainfall, and names a limitation, but offers little analysis of why, so it earns the 4 mark level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Litter items change over the six weeks, rising and then falling.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the trend in general terms without figures, so it earns the 2 mark level.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical table, not real data, for one site over six weeks. Week 1: 35 litter items, 5 mm weekly rainfall. Week 2: 40 items, 2 mm. Week 3: 52 items, 0 mm. Week 4: 48 items, 1 mm. Week 5: 30 items, 18 mm. Week 6: 25 items, 22 mm.

dotPoints.description: Interpret and analyse statistics to identify patterns, trends and relationships

prompts.question: Analyse the hypothetical data in the scenario to identify one pattern, one trend and one relationship between museum visitors and cafes, and explain what the hypothetical data cannot show about cause.
markerNotes: Give a figure with each claim. A pattern is a repeated feature (both variables dip in 2020), a trend is the direction over the whole period, and a relationship is how the two variables move together.
The strongest answers separate association from cause: visitors and cafes rising together does not show that one drives the other, and a shared factor such as a festival could explain both.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that more cafes cause more visitors because both rose, without acknowledging that the data cannot show cause.
Quoting raw values such as 55 500 visitors without calculating or describing the change over time.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Identifies one pattern, one trend and one relationship from the hypothetical data, supports each with correct figures or a percentage change, and explains that correlation does not show which variable causes the other or whether a third factor drives both
5 marks: Identifies a pattern, a trend and a relationship with figures, but the explanation of what the data cannot show is missing or vague
4 marks: Identifies two of the three features (pattern, trend, relationship) with some correct figures
3 marks: Describes the change in one variable without linking it to the other
2 marks: States one feature of the data with a single correct figure
1 mark: Restates one value from the scenario without interpreting it

sampleAnswers.answer: The hypothetical data show a clear pattern: museum visitors and cafes move in the same direction in each of the four year-to-year changes. Both rise from 2018 to 2019, both fall in 2020, and both rise in 2021 and 2022. The overall trend is upward for both. Visitors grew from 42 000 to 55 500, a rise of about 32 per cent, while cafes grew from 9 to 13, a rise of about 44 per cent, so cafes grew faster in proportional terms. The relationship is positive, because the years with more visitors are also the years with more cafes. However, the hypothetical data cannot show which variable causes the other. More cafes may attract visitors, or more visitors may encourage new cafes to open, and a shared factor such as a festival could drive both. Five years is too short to establish a reliable link.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a pattern, a trend and a relationship, supports each with correct figures and percentage change, and explains that the data show association rather than cause. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: Visitor numbers rose from 42 000 to 55 500 over the five years, so there is an upward trend. Visitors and cafes both fell in 2020, which is a pattern. Cafes also increased over the period, so the two are connected in some way.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a trend and a pattern with correct figures, but the relationship is only implied and the data's limits are not discussed. Two of the three features are identified, which earns 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Visitors rose to 55 500 by 2022.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives one correct figure from the scenario but does not identify a pattern, trend or relationship. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical data for a small coastal town over five years. Museum visitors and cafes on the main street: 2018, 42 000 visitors and 9 cafes; 2019, 46 500 visitors and 10 cafes; 2020, 39 000 visitors and 8 cafes; 2021, 51 000 visitors and 12 cafes; 2022, 55 500 visitors and 13 cafes.

prompts.question: Assess the reliability of the hypothetical correlation between canopy cover and surface temperature in the scenario, and the extent to which it supports a conclusion about cause.
markerNotes: Assess weighs evidence against conclusions: name the limitations, then judge how far they weaken the claim. A stronger answer does not dismiss the r value entirely.
Watch for the outlier: one suburb with very high temperature and low canopy can change r, so the answer should test whether the relationship holds without it.
commonStudentErrors: Treating r = −0.41 as proof that canopy cover causes lower temperatures, without considering confounding factors such as building density or surface materials.
Describing the scatter pattern without judging its reliability, for example by overlooking that only 12 suburbs are sampled.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Assesses the reliability of the correlation using the small sample of 12 suburbs, the influence of the outlier and the single-date satellite data, explains that correlation does not establish cause, and reaches a supported judgement
5-6 marks: Assesses reliability using one or two of these limitations and explains why correlation does not show cause, with a basic judgement on what the data can and cannot establish
4 marks: Describes the correlation and makes one relevant comment on its reliability or on cause, without a developed assessment
2-3 marks: States the value and direction of r, and may add a brief comment, but does not assess reliability or cause
1 mark: Names the correlation without interpreting it

sampleAnswers.answer: The correlation of −0.41 indicates a moderate negative association: suburbs with more canopy cover tend to have lower afternoon surface temperatures. The reliability of this result is limited in several ways. First, the sample is only 12 suburbs, so the value of r is sensitive to a small number of cases, and a different set of suburbs could produce a noticeably different coefficient. Second, the industrial estate with 4 per cent canopy is an outlier, sitting far from the trend, and its very high temperature may be driving much of the negative relationship. The analyst should recalculate the correlation without it to test whether the association holds for the residential suburbs. Third, the satellite data come from a single summer afternoon, so one day's weather, cloud or wind could distort the surface temperature readings. Fourth, suburbs are an arbitrary unit of analysis, so the pattern may change if different boundaries were used. This is a known problem for area data, because the result depends on how the study area is divided. On the question of cause, a correlation establishes association, not causation. Canopy cover is confounded with other variables: suburbs with many trees are often older, lower in density and have fewer dark roofs and roads, and any of these could lower surface temperature. Tree shade and evapotranspiration are plausible mechanisms, but this study does not test them directly. A more convincing test would compare suburbs of similar density and age, so that the canopy effect could be separated from those other differences. Overall, the result is a useful hypothesis that supports planting trees in hot suburbs. The hypothetical data alone, however, do not show that canopy cover causes the difference in temperature, and a judgement on cause needs a controlled comparison or a larger, multi-date study. The coefficient should therefore be treated as a starting point for investigation rather than as a finding, and stated with appropriate caution. The check is worthwhile because it tests whether the reported association is robust to the choices made in the analysis.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Assesses reliability using the small sample, the outlier and the single-date data, explains why correlation is not causation with a confounding example, and reaches a supported judgement. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The correlation of −0.41 shows a moderate negative relationship: suburbs with more canopy tend to be cooler. However, the sample is only 12 suburbs, which is small, and the industrial estate is an outlier, so the result may not be reliable. The data show association rather than cause, because other features of the suburbs could also lower temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the sample size and the outlier as limitations, with a basic judgement that the data show association rather than cause. This earns 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The value of r is −0.41, which is a negative correlation between canopy cover and temperature.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the value and direction of the correlation without assessing reliability or cause. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical study of 12 suburbs in a large city. Tree canopy cover ranges from 4 to 38 per cent. The correlation between canopy cover and afternoon surface temperature is r = −0.41. One suburb, an industrial estate with 4 per cent canopy, has the highest temperature and sits well away from the trend. The study uses satellite data from a single summer afternoon.

dotPoints.description: Use GPS to collect location data

prompts.question: Describe how a handheld GPS receiver is used to collect the location of each tree in the hypothetical school grounds survey, including the steps taken before and after each point is recorded.
markerNotes: Describe means say how and in what order, not just what. Sequence the steps from switching on, to fixing satellites, to recording points and transferring data.
A strong answer adds that the accuracy reading should be checked before recording, because handheld receivers vary in accuracy and a poor fix will shift every point.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what GPS is in general terms rather than the steps used to collect each tree's location.
Forgetting to mention that the receiver needs a clear view of the sky to obtain a satellite fix.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Describes the steps in order: switching on and waiting for a satellite fix, checking the accuracy reading, recording and labelling each waypoint, repeating for each tree, and then transferring the coordinates to a GIS
4 marks: Describes the main steps of GPS collection but omits the check on accuracy or the data transfer
3 marks: Describes that the receiver records coordinates for each tree, without the steps
2 marks: Identifies GPS as a tool that gives location, with a brief comment
1 mark: Names GPS without describing its use

sampleAnswers.answer: The student switches on the handheld GPS receiver in an open area with a clear view of the sky and waits for a satellite fix. Before recording, the student checks the accuracy reading on the screen and waits until it stabilises, because poor accuracy shifts every point. The student then stands beside each tree, takes the reading and saves it as a labelled waypoint, such as the tree's number and species. If a reading is unstable, the student moves to a more open spot and records again. This is repeated for all 40 trees. Back in the classroom, the waypoints are downloaded and the coordinates are transferred into the GIS as a point layer, where each tree's location data can be linked to its attributes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the steps in order, including the accuracy check, the waypoint recording for each tree and the transfer of coordinates into a GIS. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: The GPS receiver records the coordinates of each tree, so the location of every tree can be mapped later in the GIS.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes what the receiver records and why it is useful, but not the steps taken before and after each reading. This earns 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: GPS gives the location of each tree.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names what the GPS provides without describing how it is used. This earns 1 mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical Year 11 fieldwork in a school grounds park. Students record the location of 40 trees with a handheld GPS receiver before mapping them in a GIS.

prompts.question: Justify the use of GPS to collect the locations of the hypothetical high-water marks, and evaluate the sources of positional error that could reduce its usefulness under the forest canopy.
markerNotes: Justify needs reasons for the choice: GPS gives coordinates for each mark, can be transferred into a GIS, and is much quicker than traversing a wide, wet valley with a tape and compass.
Evaluate the error sources by how they affect this survey: dense canopy weakens the satellite signal, and reflections off wet trunks and the river can add positional error.
commonStudentErrors: Asserting that GPS is always accurate, so the answer never considers the effect of the canopy.
Listing sources of error without linking any of them to the forested valley in the scenario.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Justifies GPS as the appropriate tool for mapping the marks, weighs at least two sources of positional error, such as canopy blocking satellite signals and multipath reflection from trunks and water, against remedies such as differential correction, and reaches a supported judgement
5-6 marks: Justifies GPS with a reason and evaluates one or two sources of positional error with explanation, though remedies and a supported judgement are missing or underdeveloped
4 marks: Describes GPS and names a source of error with some explanation, without justifying its use for the survey
2-3 marks: States that GPS gives the location of each mark, with a brief comment on accuracy, but no justification or evaluation
1 mark: Names GPS without comment

sampleAnswers.answer: GPS is justified as the main method for this survey because it gives a coordinate for each high-water mark that can be transferred directly into a GIS, and it is far faster than tape-and-compass traversing across a wide, wet valley. Surveyors can record the marks in a single pass, and the coordinates can then be checked against the observed flood extent. However, the value of GPS depends on the conditions, and the forest canopy presents the greatest problem. Dense canopy blocks or weakens the satellite signals, so the receiver may take longer to fix a position, or it may record a position with much lower accuracy. Multipath error is also significant: signals reflected off wet tree trunks, the water surface and the valley walls take longer to reach the receiver than the direct signal, which shifts the calculated position. Satellite geometry adds to the problem, because under a canopy the receiver often sees fewer satellites spread across the sky, which weakens the fix. These errors matter because the purpose of the survey is to show exactly where the flood reached, so a position several metres out could place a mark on the wrong side of a boundary. Surveyors can reduce the error by leaving the receiver to average its readings for longer, by recording in the more open areas where possible, and by applying differential correction, which uses a reference station to remove part of the error. Multipath is hard to remove entirely, so surveyors may also repeat readings from different positions and compare them, which exposes readings that are out of line. The GPS data should therefore be presented with an accuracy estimate for each point, so that anyone using the flood map can judge the reliability of each mark. Without these steps the canopy would make GPS a weaker choice in this valley, so the survey should record the accuracy of each point, report where the positional error is largest, and state the remaining uncertainty in the mapped flood extent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies GPS with clear reasons, evaluates canopy blocking and multipath as sources of positional error, and weighs remedies such as differential correction against the purpose of the survey. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: GPS is a suitable tool because it records the coordinates of each high-water mark and can be transferred into a GIS. Under the dense forest canopy, however, the receiver may lose satellite signals, so its position may be less accurate. This makes the data less reliable where the canopy is closed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies GPS with a reason and names one source of error (the canopy) with an explanation, but does not evaluate a remedy or reach a judgement. This earns 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: GPS gives the location of each mark. It can be less accurate under trees.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States what GPS provides and a brief comment on accuracy, without justification or evaluation. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical flood-mapping survey of a forested river valley. Surveyors must record the exact location of 80 high-water marks left on tree trunks. Much of the valley floor is under a dense, closed canopy, and the river is wide and bordered by wet ground.

dotPoints.description: Represent spatial information in a variety of forms

prompts.question: Differentiate between a choropleth map and a proportional symbol map as ways of representing the hypothetical hospital visits data in the scenario.
markerNotes: Differentiate means identify the difference and what it changes for the reader. Name the basis of each map (area shading versus symbol size) and what the reader is drawn to compare.
A strong answer notes that choropleth maps depend on the area boundaries chosen, while proportional symbols show the value at a point, which can be clearer when the values are counts.
commonStudentErrors: Describing each map without saying how they differ.
Confusing the two: calling the shaded map a proportional symbol map, or treating symbol size and colour class as the same kind of encoding.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains that a choropleth map shades whole areas by class and a proportional symbol map scales symbols to values at points, and states the effect of each on how the hospital visits data are read, with an example from the scenario
3 marks: States the key difference between the two maps and gives one example, without the effect on reading the data
2 marks: Describes one map type correctly, without comparison
1 mark: Names one map type

sampleAnswers.answer: A choropleth map and a proportional symbol map both show spatial information, but they encode the hospital visits data differently. A choropleth map shades each suburb by a class range, such as low, medium or high visits per 1 000 residents, so the reader compares the shade of whole areas, and large suburbs can look more prominent even when their rates are low. A proportional symbol map places a circle at a point in each suburb, scaled to the value, so the reader compares the size of symbols. This shows the value at each location without the suburb's area distorting the impression.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the basis of each map, the effect on what the reader compares, and the example of the hospital visits data. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: A choropleth map shades each suburb by class, so darker shades show higher visit rates. A proportional symbol map uses larger circles for suburbs with more visits. The choropleth shows the rate for each area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the key difference and gives an example of each map, but does not explain the effect on how the data are read. This earns 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A choropleth map uses colours.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names a feature of one map type without comparison. This earns 1 mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical dataset of emergency hospital visits per 1 000 residents in six suburbs of a regional city, to be shown on a map for the local health service.

prompts.question: Evaluate the suitability of three of these forms of spatial representation for communicating flood risk to residents with no GIS training, and recommend the form most likely to change residents' decisions about their property.
markerNotes: Evaluate means weigh strengths against weaknesses for a stated audience. Here the audience is residents with no GIS training, so the criteria are clarity, accuracy and whether residents can act on the information.

A recommendation needs a reason tied to behaviour change: a map that shows whether a resident's own property is affected may be stronger than a classed choropleth, even if the choropleth is easier to make.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the forms without evaluating them against the audience.
Recommending the interactive web GIS without acknowledging that residents with no GIS training may find it hard to use.
prompts.markingCriteria:
9-10 marks: Evaluates three forms against the needs of residents with no GIS training (clarity of the legend, the depth information shown, and the risk of misreading classes), justifies a recommendation with evidence, and identifies a limitation of the recommended form
7-8 marks: Evaluates three forms with clear reasons and recommends one with some justification
6 marks: Evaluates at least two forms and makes a recommendation without linking it to the audience
4-5 marks: Describes the features of two or three forms and states which is best, without reasons
2-3 marks: Describes one form and one of its features
1 mark: Names a form of spatial representation

sampleAnswers.answer: Each of the forms of spatial representation considered here has a different strength for communicating flood risk to residents with no GIS training. The choropleth map of flood-risk classes by street is easy to read at a glance, because darker streets signal higher risk, and a single legend can explain the classes. However, the classes are a generalisation: a street with mixed risk is shaded as one value, and the boundaries between classes can make small differences look large. Residents may read a shaded street as uniformly dangerous or uniformly safe, which can mislead their judgement about their own property. The proportional symbol map of properties at risk is more personal, because each symbol marks a home, so a resident can see whether their own property is affected. Its weakness is that symbol sizes are hard to compare when many properties overlap, and it shows the number of properties rather than the depth of water a resident would face. The annotated photograph with a hand-drawn overlay can be read by many residents without training, because the street and the houses are recognisable, and the overlay can mark the flood extent in a way that anchors the risk to a place they know. Its limits are that it cannot be scaled to the whole city and that a hand-drawn overlay may look less authoritative and is harder to verify. The interactive web GIS would allow residents to explore depth layers for their own address, but residents with no GIS training may find it difficult to operate, and its many layers can overwhelm a casual user. Of the forms considered, the annotated photograph is the most suitable for behaviour change at the individual level, because it links the risk to a recognisable property and can be read without training. It should be paired with a simple legend showing flood depth, and its main limitation is that it is only reliable for the area it covers, so residents outside the photograph may not see their own risk. The choropleth map is the best complement for the wider picture, but it should not be the only form used with this audience, because a single classed map can hide the variation that matters most to an individual household. A useful test is to ask residents, before publication, which form they can use to find their own street and explain what the risk means for them, because that test reflects the audience more directly than any technical criterion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates three forms against the needs of residents with no GIS training, recommends the annotated photograph with a reason tied to behaviour change, and identifies its limitation. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The annotated photograph is the most useful form for residents with no GIS training, because the houses and streets are familiar and the flood extent is marked on them. The choropleth map is easy to read but shades whole streets, which can hide differences between properties. The interactive web GIS is powerful but may be too complicated for most residents.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Evaluates three forms against the audience with clear reasons and recommends one with some justification, but the recommendation is not tied closely to behaviour change and the limitation of the recommended form is not given. This earns 7 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A choropleth map shades streets by flood risk class.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one form and one of its features without evaluation. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical council flood-risk project. Planners must explain to residents which streets face the greatest flood risk. Four options are considered: a choropleth map of flood-risk classes by street, a proportional symbol map of properties at risk, an interactive web GIS with layers for flood depth, and an annotated photograph with a hand-drawn overlay. Most residents have no GIS training.

dotPoints.description: Use data to create maps and map layers

prompts.question: Outline the steps a class would follow to turn the field-checked land use records into a map layer in the GIS, from data entry to a finished map.
markerNotes: Outline means give the main steps briefly, in order. You do not need detail on each step, but each step should be a recognisable stage in the process.
A strong answer includes a check against the photograph, since errors in the field records would otherwise carry into every map made from the layer.
commonStudentErrors: Listing software functions without describing the process of making a map layer.
Skipping the step of assigning each record to a land use class, so the map has no categories to display.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the steps in order: entering each record into the attribute table with its coordinates, assigning land use classes, applying symbology with a legend, and checking the layer against the photograph before printing
3 marks: Outlines three of these steps in a sensible order
2 marks: Outlines two steps without order or purpose
1 mark: Names GIS or map layer without steps

sampleAnswers.answer: First, the field records are entered through data entry into the GIS, with each point's coordinates and field notes stored in the attribute table. Second, each point is assigned to a land use class, using the categories agreed before fieldwork. Third, the class field sets the symbology, so each class has its own colour, and a legend is added to match symbols to meanings. Finally, the map layer is checked against the aerial photograph for points in the wrong place or class, and the corrected layer is printed with a title, scale and north arrow.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines the steps in order from data entry through classification and symbology to the check against the photograph, which meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: First, the field records are entered into the attribute table with their coordinates. Next, each point is assigned to a land use class. Finally, the layer is displayed with symbols and a legend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines three steps in a sensible order, but does not include the check against the photograph. This earns 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Use GIS to make the map.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Names the tool without outlining any steps. This earns 1 mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical Year 11 project. Students have field-checked the land use at 60 points on an aerial photograph and want to turn these records into a land use map layer in a GIS.

prompts.question: Discuss how decisions about the classification method, symbology and layer order affect the way a GIS map layer represents the spatial pattern of flood depth in the hypothetical suburb.
markerNotes: Discuss needs both sides: the effect of each choice on the picture a reader sees, and why that effect matters. Link each decision to the spatial pattern, not just to the software option.

Equal intervals can make the pattern look flatter or more dramatic depending on the range of the data, while natural breaks group values where they cluster. A strong answer explains which choice suits the purpose of the map.
commonStudentErrors: Describing how to use the symbology tool rather than discussing its effect on the flood depth pattern.
Stating that natural breaks are always more accurate, without considering the purpose of the map.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Discusses how the classification choice (equal intervals versus natural breaks) changes the apparent pattern of flood depth, how symbology and layer order affect legibility and emphasis, and reaches a supported view on which choices suit a public audience
5-6 marks: Discusses two of the three decisions with reasons for their effect on the pattern
4 marks: Describes one decision and its effect on the map, with a brief reason
2-3 marks: Describes the map layer and one feature of its classification or symbology
1 mark: Names one GIS decision without its effect

sampleAnswers.answer: The way flood depth is classed in the map layer changes the pattern a reader sees, so classification is the most influential of the three decisions. Equal intervals divide the depth range into classes of the same width, which is simple to explain, but if most properties fall in one narrow band, the map will show a few classes with many features and make the rest of the pattern look uniform. Natural breaks group the values where the data cluster, so the classes reflect the distribution of depths in the suburb and are more likely to reveal the difference between the shallow and deep parts of the flood. The same flood depth values can therefore look very different in the two versions, and a reader could reach a different view of which streets are most at risk. Symbology affects how the classes are read. A sequential colour scheme from light to dark suits flood depth, because the order of the colours matches the order of the values, whereas a diverging or rainbow scheme may suggest a break in the data that does not exist. Colour choices also affect legibility for readers with colour vision deficiency, and a clear legend is needed for any scheme. Layer order determines what is visible and what is emphasised. If the flood depth layer is placed beneath the property boundaries, the boundaries may hide the depth colours. If the drainage lines are placed above the flood depth layer, they may guide the eye to the channels and make the flood pattern look concentrated along them. A sensible order puts the flood depth layer at the base, with the drainage lines and property boundaries drawn above it in thin, contrasting lines. Taken together, these decisions shape the pattern a reader perceives, so the mapmaker must justify each choice. For a public audience, natural breaks combined with a sequential scheme and a suitable layer order are likely to give the clearest impression of the pattern, provided the classes and their meaning are explained clearly in the legend.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses how the classification choice changes the apparent pattern, how symbology and layer order affect legibility and emphasis, and reaches a supported view for a public audience. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Equal intervals and natural breaks can produce different classes from the same flood depth data, so the same suburb may look more or less at risk. A sequential colour scheme suits depth values, and a legend is needed so readers can match the colours to the classes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses two of the three decisions with reasons for their effect on the pattern, but does not cover the third. This earns 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The GIS has a map layer for flood depth, classed into three groups and shown with colours.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes the map layer and one feature of its classification and symbology, without discussing effect. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical flood-risk study of a low-lying suburb. Analysts build a set of GIS map layers: property boundaries, ground elevation, flood depth in three classes and drainage lines. In one version flood depth is classed using equal intervals; in another it is classed using natural breaks.

dotPoints.description: Use spatial technologies to calculate, analyse and compare patterns, distributions and densities

prompts.question: Calculate the density of bus shelters in each of the two hypothetical suburbs, showing your working, and state which suburb has the higher density.
markerNotes: Density is the count divided by the area, so divide the number of shelters by the area in square kilometres, and show each division.
Check that the answer is sensible: the suburb with more shelters is not always the denser one, because the area matters.
commonStudentErrors: Dividing the area by the count, which inverts the ratio and gives 0.11 rather than 9.
Comparing raw counts (36 versus 12) and concluding that Suburb A is denser, without dividing by area.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Calculates both densities correctly (9 per square kilometre for Suburb A and 8 per square kilometre for Suburb B), shows the division for each, and states that Suburb A has the higher density
3 marks: Calculates both densities with one error in the working or the units, and states the higher suburb
2 marks: Calculates one density correctly and shows the method
1 mark: States the method of dividing the count by the area, without calculation

sampleAnswers.answer: Density is the number of bus shelters divided by the area they cover, so each count is divided by its area in square kilometres. For Suburb A, 36 bus shelters ÷ 4 square kilometres = 9 bus shelters per square kilometre. For Suburb B, 12 bus shelters ÷ 1.5 square kilometres = 8 bus shelters per square kilometre. Suburb A therefore has the higher density, at 9 compared with 8 per square kilometre. The difference is small, but a GIS can confirm the pattern by counting the shelters in each suburb and dividing by its calculated area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Shows both divisions with units, gives the densities of 9 and 8 per square kilometre, and states that Suburb A is denser. Full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Suburb A: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 bus shelters per square kilometre. Suburb B: 12 ÷ 1.5 = 7 bus shelters per square kilometre. Suburb A has the higher density.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Calculates both densities with one arithmetic error in Suburb B (12 ÷ 1.5 is 8), and states the higher suburb correctly. This earns 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Density is the number of shelters divided by the area.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States the method without calculating either density. This earns 1 mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical GIS analysis of bus shelters. Suburb A covers 4 square kilometres and contains 36 bus shelters. Suburb B covers 1.5 square kilometres and contains 12 bus shelters.

prompts.question: Justify the use of kernel density estimation rather than counts per suburb to compare the density of potholes across the hypothetical city, and identify one choice that can change the result.
markerNotes: Justify needs reasons for the choice, not just a description. Link the reason to the problem: suburbs of very different sizes distort counts per suburb.
The choice that changes the result should be specific: a larger search radius smooths the surface and can merge separate clusters, hiding local hotspots.
commonStudentErrors: Describing how kernel density works without explaining why it is preferable in this case.
Naming the search radius as a choice but not stating its effect on the pattern.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies kernel density by explaining that it uses the exact point locations and is not distorted by unequal suburb sizes, and identifies a choice (such as the search radius) that alters the surface and so the apparent pattern
5 marks: Justifies the method with one reason and identifies a choice that changes the result, with a brief explanation
4 marks: Justifies the method with one reason, without identifying a choice
3 marks: Describes kernel density or counts per suburb, with one comparison
2 marks: States one feature of either method
1 mark: Names kernel density without description

sampleAnswers.answer: Kernel density estimation answers the council's question, where potholes are concentrated, more directly than counts per suburb. Each of the 420 reported potholes is used as exact point data, and the surface shows how many potholes lie within a neighbourhood of each location, so the density distribution follows the real locations of the damage. Counts per suburb are distorted by suburb boundaries: a large suburb with few potholes may look sparse, while a small suburb may look severe only because its boundary happens to enclose a cluster. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, in which the result depends on the boundaries drawn. The choice that changes the result is the search radius. A small radius reveals local hotspots but produces a noisy surface, while a large radius smooths the surface and can merge two separate clusters, hiding the concentration the council needs to see. The council should report the radius used and test two or three values before relying on the pattern. A surface is also easier for a non-specialist audience to read than a table of counts. Mapping the surface back onto the 420 reported potholes lets the council check that each hotspot is supported by real points.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies kernel density with the point-based reason and the problem of unequal suburb sizes, and identifies the search radius as a choice that alters the apparent pattern. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: Kernel density is better than counts per suburb because the suburbs are very different sizes, so counts can be misleading. The kernel surface uses each pothole's exact location, so the pattern is not forced into suburb boundaries.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Justifies the method with one reason tied to suburb size, but does not identify a choice that changes the result. This earns 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Kernel density shows the density of potholes using a surface.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States one feature of the method without justification. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical city council GIS analysis of 420 reported potholes. Analysts compare two approaches: counting potholes per suburb, which uses boundaries that differ greatly in size, and a kernel density surface, which estimates density from each point and its neighbours using a search radius that the analyst sets.

dotPoints.description: Use spatial information to determine connections, impacts and change over time

prompts.question: Explain how a series of satellite images can be used to determine connections, impacts and change over time in the hypothetical river catchment.
markerNotes: Explain means how and why: say how comparing dated images reveals change, and how overlaying land and river layers reveals connections.
Impacts are inferred from the images, so a strong answer notes that field checks such as water sampling or channel measurements confirm what the images suggest.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what changed without explaining how the images show it.
Claiming that satellite images show impacts directly, when impacts such as sediment loading need additional evidence.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains that the image series is compared at the same time of year to remove seasonal effects, that change over time is identified by comparing dates, that connections are made by overlaying land use and river channel layers, and that impacts are inferred and checked against field evidence
5 marks: Explains how the images are compared over time and how connections or impacts are identified, with minimal detail on method
4 marks: Explains that images are compared over time and identifies one connection or impact
3 marks: Describes the change shown by the images, without method
2 marks: States one feature of satellite images
1 mark: Names satellite images as a source

sampleAnswers.answer: Satellite images show change over time because each image records the same catchment on a different date, and comparing them in sequence shows what has altered. The images are taken at the same time of year, so that seasonal differences in vegetation and water levels are not mistaken for long-term change. Each image is classified into land use types, and the classes are compared to measure how much each has grown or shrunk over the 15 years. Connections are shown by overlaying these layers in the GIS: land parcel boundaries show whether clearing follows parcel lines, and river channels show whether clearing is close to the channel. Impacts are inferred from the pattern, for example bare soil beside a channel may suggest more sediment entering the river. This inference is not proven by the images alone, so it must be checked against field evidence such as water sampling.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains how dated images show change over time, how overlays on land parcels and channels reveal connections, and how impacts are inferred and then checked in the field. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: The satellite images are compared over time, so the analyst can see that cleared land along the river increased between the early and later images. Overlaying the river channels shows that much of the clearing is near the banks, which is a connection between land use and the river.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains that the images are compared over time and identifies one connection, but does not explain the role of the field checks or the seasonal timing. This earns 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Satellite images show the land surface at different dates.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States one feature of satellite images without explaining how they show change or connections. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical river catchment studied with a series of satellite images taken at the same time of year over 15 years. A GIS overlays the images on land parcel boundaries and river channels.

prompts.question: Evaluate the extent to which the satellite images and the GIS layer establish connections between the hypothetical port expansion and the change in mangrove cover over time, and identify what the images cannot show about impacts.
markerNotes: Evaluate needs a judgement: the images can show that mangrove cover changed and that the change coincides with the expansion, but a match in time and place is not proof of connection.
Impacts such as changes in water quality or sediment need ground data that the scenario lacks. Naming the missing evidence strengthens the evaluation.
commonStudentErrors: Assuming that because the change followed the expansion, the port caused it.
Ignoring the absence of water quality data when judging impacts.
prompts.markingCriteria:
9-10 marks: Evaluates how far the overlay and the time series can establish a connection, weighing the strength of the temporal evidence against the lack of water quality data, identifies what the images cannot show about impacts, and reaches a supported judgement
7-8 marks: Evaluates the connection with reasons and identifies at least one limit on impacts
6 marks: Explains how the images show change over time and links it to the expansion, with an evaluative comment
4-5 marks: Describes change in mangrove cover and the expansion, with an unsupported claim of connection
2-3 marks: States one piece of evidence from the scenario
1 mark: Names the satellite images or the GIS layer

sampleAnswers.answer: The connections between the port expansion and the change over time in mangrove cover can be tested with the satellite images and the GIS layer. The satellite images and the GIS layer can establish a plausible connection between the expansion and the loss of mangrove cover, but they cannot establish that the expansion caused the change. The strongest evidence is the temporal sequence. Images from 2005, 2012 and 2020 allow the analyst to measure when mangrove cover changed, and if the sharpest loss falls between two dates that bracket the construction period, the timing supports a connection. The GIS layer adds spatial strength: when the footprint of the expansion is overlaid on the classified images, the analyst can show whether mangrove loss is concentrated near the new structures or spread across the estuary. A loss of mangroves within or immediately beside the footprint is far stronger evidence than a loss scattered across the whole estuary, which could reflect other pressures. However, the evidence has three weaknesses. First, three dates are few, so the analyst cannot be sure that the change between 2012 and 2020 is not part of a longer natural fluctuation in cover. Second, mangrove cover is influenced by sediment, tides, sea level and storms, and the satellite images cannot separate these influences from the effect of the expansion. Third, the images record cover, not processes, so they cannot show whether the loss is caused by dredging, changes to tidal flow or pollution. The absence of water quality data is a critical gap, because it means the images cannot show impacts on the estuary's chemistry or on the species that depend on mangroves. The images can show the outline of an impact, such as cleared mangroves beside the port, but not its consequences for water, fish or sediment. A judgement on connection therefore depends on whether the overlay and the timing support one another. If both do, the evidence supports a connection that should be tested with water sampling and mangrove health surveys before any causal claim is made. The images alone establish association, and the impacts remain unmeasured. A useful next step would be to compare the timing of the loss with tidal records and rainfall, because a sudden loss after a storm would point to a different cause from a gradual loss that follows the construction schedule. Such a comparison would strengthen or weaken the connection, and it would show whether the expansion is the most likely explanation among several. The result should be stated as a judgement with its uncertainty, so that the council can decide whether more monitoring is needed before acting.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Weighs the timing and spatial overlay as evidence for a connection against the three weaknesses and the missing water quality data, names what the images cannot show about impacts, and reaches a supported judgement. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The images show mangrove cover falling between 2012 and 2020, and the GIS layer shows the port expansion beside the estuary, so there is a connection in time and place. However, the images cannot show what caused the loss, and there is no water quality data to show impacts.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the change over time and links it to the expansion, with an evaluative comment on the limits of the evidence. This earns 6 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The satellite images are from 2005, 2012 and 2020.
sampleAnswers.feedback: States one piece of evidence from the scenario without evaluation. This earns 2 marks.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical port expansion beside a mangrove-lined estuary. The council holds satellite images from 2005, 2012 and 2020 and a GIS layer of the expansion footprint. No water quality samples are available for the period.

dotPoints.description: Estimate the scale of aerial photographs and satellite images

prompts.question: Calculate the scale of the hypothetical aerial photograph in the scenario, using the netball court of known length, and show your working.
markerNotes: Scale is the photograph distance compared with the ground distance, so both must be in the same units before dividing: 30 metres is 3000 centimetres.
State the scale as a ratio, 1:500, not as 500, because the representative fraction keeps the units consistent and is the form used on maps and photographs.
commonStudentErrors: Leaving the ground distance in metres while the photograph distance is in centimetres, which gives a wrong scale.
Writing 500 as the answer, without expressing the scale as a ratio.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Converts 30 metres to 3000 centimetres, divides the ground distance by the photograph distance to give 3000 ÷ 6 = 500, and states the scale as 1:500 with the working shown
3 marks: Converts the units correctly but makes an error in the division, and states the method
2 marks: States that scale is the photograph distance over the ground distance, with one correct conversion
1 mark: Identifies the ground distance and the photograph distance without calculation

sampleAnswers.answer: The netball court is 30 metres long, which is 3000 centimetres, so the ground distance and the photograph distance must be in the same units before the scale is calculated. The court measures 6 centimetres on the aerial photograph. The scale is the ground distance divided by the photograph distance: 3000 ÷ 6 = 500, so the scale is 1:500. This means that 1 centimetre on the photograph represents 500 centimetres on the ground. Checking the answer, 6 centimetres multiplied by 500 gives 3000 centimetres, which is the 30 metres we started from.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Converts the units before dividing, shows the division giving 500, states the scale as 1:500 and checks the result. This meets the full-mark criteria.

sampleAnswers.answer: Scale is the ground distance divided by the photograph distance. 30 metres is 3000 centimetres, and 3000 ÷ 6 = 50, so the scale is 1:50.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Converts the units correctly and states the method, but makes a division error (3000 ÷ 6 is 500, not 50). This earns 3 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The netball court is 30 metres long and 6 centimetres on the photograph.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the two distances without calculating a scale. This earns 1 mark.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical aerial photograph of a school. For this exercise, a netball court is taken to be 30 metres long, and it measures 6 centimetres in length on the photograph.

prompts.question: Assess the reliability of estimating scale from the aerial photograph and from the satellite image of this steeply undulating terrain in the hypothetical study area.
markerNotes: Assess needs a judgement about how far each estimate can be trusted: a nominal scale on an aerial photograph is exact only on the flat reference plane.
Relief displacement is the key term for aerial photographs; orthorectified satellite products have been corrected for terrain, so the answer should also say what uncertainty remains.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the nominal scale of 1:25 000 as accurate everywhere in the photograph.
Stating that satellite images have no distortion, without considering terrain or viewing angle.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Assesses the reliability of each scale estimate, explaining that relief displacement distorts the scale of the aerial photograph across uneven terrain and that orthorectification corrects satellite image geometry, and reaches a supported, conditional judgement on which estimate is more reliable
5-6 marks: Explains relief displacement or orthorectification and its effect on the scale, and assesses one or both estimates with a reason, but without a full comparison or a supported judgement
4 marks: Describes how scale is estimated from one data source, with one comment on the effect of terrain, but without explaining relief displacement or orthorectification
2-3 marks: States the nominal scale or pixel size of a data source, with a brief comment on terrain, but with no assessment of reliability
1 mark: Names a data source without comment

sampleAnswers.answer: The reliability of the two scale estimates differs because of how each image is geometrically constructed. The aerial photograph has a nominal scale of 1:25 000, but that figure is only exact on a flat reference plane at a specific elevation. On steeply undulating terrain, points higher than the reference plane are displaced outward from the centre of the photograph, and points lower than it are displaced inward. This is relief displacement, and it means the scale varies across the image. A distance measured on a steep slope or near a ridge can therefore be substantially different from the same distance measured on the valley floor, so the nominal scale is reliable only for the flat parts of the image and is unreliable for measuring distances across the ridges. The analyst would need to correct the photograph using a digital elevation model, or to measure distances between points at the same height. The satellite image has a 10-metre pixel size, which gives a precise grid, but a pixel size is not the same as accuracy. An unprocessed satellite image also contains geometric distortion from the sensor's viewing angle and from the terrain.
